positive_text: \text{Let } ABCD \text{ be a convex quadrilateral. If squares are constructed externally on each side with centers labeled } E, F, G, H \text{ for sides } AB, BC, CD, DA \text{ respectively, prove that the segments connecting the centers of the squares on opposite sides, } EG \text{ and } FH, \text{ are equal and perpendicular.}

negatives.text: \text{Let } ABCD \text{ be a convex quadrilateral. Squares with centers } E, F, G, H \text{ are constructed on the outside of the sides } AB, BC, CD, \text{ and } DA \text{ respectively. Show that } EG \text{ and } FH \text{ are equal and parallel.}

\text{Let } ABCD \text{ be a convex quadrilateral. Squares with centers } E, F, G, H \text{ are constructed on the inside of the sides } AB, BC, CD, \text{ and } DA \text{ respectively. Show that } EG \text{ and } FH \text{ are equal and perpendicular.}

positive_text: Consider a point particle traveling in a circular billiard table with elastic boundary reflections. If the trajectory intersects a fixed point on the table at three distinct times, prove that the point lies on a periodic orbit and is thus visited infinitely often.

negatives.text: A ball moves endlessly on a circular billiard table. When it hits the edge it is reflected. Show that if it passes through a point on the table twice, then it passes through it infinitely many times.

A ball moves endlessly on an elliptical billiard table. When it hits the edge it is reflected. Show that if it passes through a point on the table three times, then it passes through it infinitely many times.

positive_text: Consider the Poincaré upper half-plane model where the boundary is a line $R$. Define the geodesics as (1) rays perpendicular to $R$, and (2) semicircles centered on $R$. Prove that for any geodesic $L$ and any point $P$ not on $L$, there exist infinitely many geodesics through $P$ that do not meet $L$. Prove that for any triangle $ABC$ in this geometry, the sum of its interior angles is strictly less than $\pi$.

negatives.text: Let $R$ be the boundary line of the Poincaré half-plane model. Define lines as (1) rays perpendicular to $R$, and (2) semicircles with centers on $R$. Show that for any line $L$ and any point $P$ not on $L$, there are infinitely many lines through $P$ that do intersect $L$. Show that for any triangle $ABC$ in this geometry, the sum of its angles is strictly greater than $\pi$.

Let the Poincaré plane be defined as before, with boundary $R$. Define lines as (1) rays perpendicular to $R$, and (2) semicircles with centers on $R$. Show that for any line $L$ and any point $P$ not on $L$, there are exactly two lines through $P$ that do not intersect $L$. Show that for any triangle $ABC$ in this geometry, the sum of its angles is exactly $\pi$.

Let the Poincaré half-plane be defined as before, with boundary $R$. Define lines as (1) rays perpendicular to $R$, and (2) full circles centered on $R$. Show that for any line $L$ and any point $P$ not on $L$, there are infinitely many lines through $P$ that do not intersect $L$. Show that for any triangle $ABC$ in this geometry, the sum of its angles is strictly less than $\pi$.

positive_text: Determine all 10-digit numbers $d_0d_1\ldots d_9$ such that for each $i$ from 0 to 9, $d_i$ equals the total count of the digit $i$ in the number.

negatives.text: Find all 10-digit numbers $a_0a_1\ldots a_9$ such that, for each $k$, $a_k$ is the number of times that the digit $k$ does not appear in the number.

positive_text: Suppose a real number is assigned to each cell of a chessboard. If each interior cell is the average of its four adjacent cells, prove that the maximum value $N$ must occur on the boundary of the board.

negatives.text: A number is written in each square of a chessboard, so that each number not on the border is the sum of the 4 neighboring numbers. Show that if the largest number is $N$, then there is a number equal to $N$ in the border squares.

positive_text: Two players, \text{A} and \text{B}, are to split a triangular prism-shaped cake, with the triangular faces parallel to the ground. \text{A} selects a point $ P $ on the upper surface. \text{B} then cuts the cake along a vertical plane passing through $ P $, and chooses which half to take. What point $ P $ should \text{A} choose to maximize their guaranteed portion of the cake?

negatives.text: A and B wish to divide a triangular prism cake with its top and bottom faces horizontal. A chooses a point $ P $ on the top face, then B cuts the cake along a plane that contains $ P $ but is not necessarily vertical. B chooses which piece to take. What point $ P $ should A choose to maximize their guaranteed share?

positive_text: Let $n$ points be placed on a sphere such that no four are coplanar. Each pair of points is connected by a segment colored either red or blue. There exists a toggle key for each point that inverts the color of all segments connected to it. It is given that for any three points, there exists a sequence of toggles to make all three connecting segments red. Prove that all segments can be made red. Determine the minimal number of toggles needed in the worst-case scenario to achieve this.

negatives.text: Given $n$ points on a sphere, no four coplanar, with each pair of points joined by a segment that is either red or blue. A key exists for each point that toggles the color of all segments incident to it. For every three points, there is a sequence of key presses that makes the three segments between them red. Show that it is possible to make all the segments red. Find the minimal number of key presses required in the best-case scenario to achieve this.

Given $n$ points on a sphere, no four coplanar, with each pair of points joined by a segment that is either red or blue. Prove that it is possible to make all the segments red. Find the minimal number of key presses required in the worst-case scenario to achieve this, assuming that each key can only be pressed once.

\sum_{k=1}^{n} d(k) \ge n\left(\sum_{k=2}^{n} \frac{1}{k}\right) \quad \text{and} \quad \sum_{k=1}^{n} d(k) \le n\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{1}{k}\right)

positive_text: Each cell in an $n \times n$ grid contains a real number $x$ such that $|x| < 1$, and every $2 \times 2$ subgrid has total sum zero. Prove that if $n$ is odd, the total sum of all numbers in the grid is strictly less than $n$.

positive_text:
Given an infinite sequence of glasses with $n$ stones in the central glass (glass $0$), consider two types of moves:

• Move $A'$: If there are at least one stone in glass $i$ and at least one in glass $i+1$, one can move one stone from glass $i+1$ to glass $i-1$ and remove one stone from glass $i$.

• Move $B'$: If there are at least two stones in glass $i$, one can transfer one stone from glass $i$ to glass $i+2$ and another to glass $i-1$.

Show that by repeatedly applying $A'$ and $B'$, the system will always reach a state where no more moves are possible. Moreover, prove that this terminal state is uniquely determined by the initial configuration.

negatives.text:
One has a long row of glasses and $n$ stones in the central glass (glass $0$). The following movements are allowed:

• Movement $A$
If there is at least one stone in glass $i$ and at least one in glass $i+1$, one may move one stone from glass $i+1$ to glass $i+1$ (no change), and remove one from glass $i$.

• Movement $B$
If there are at least two stones in glass $i$, one may move one stone from glass $i$ to glass $i+1$ and another to glass $i-1$.

Prove that repeated application of these movements leads to a stable configuration.

• Movement $B$

Prove that repeated application of these movements leads to a stable configuration.

One has a long row of glasses and $n$ stones in the central glass (glass $0$). The following movements are allowed:

• Movement $B$
If there are at least two stones in glass $i$, one may move one stone from glass $i$ to glass $i+2$ and one from glass $i+1$ to glass $i-1$.

Prove that repeated application of these movements leads to a stable configuration.

positive_text:
A professora Jacira propõe um jogo na lousa:
I) Um aluno escreve uma sequência com $n$ dígitos não nulos;
II) Outro aluno cria uma nova sequência com $(n-1)$ dígitos, onde cada termo é a diferença positiva entre dois elementos consecutivos da sequência anterior;
III) Um terceiro aluno repete o processo com a nova sequência;
IV) O processo prossegue até que reste apenas um dígito.
V) Se qualquer sequência contiver um zero, o processo é interrompido e chamamos a sequência de FURADA.
Por exemplo:

| $1^\circ$ aluno | 5 | 8 | 9 |   |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| $2^\circ$ aluno | 3 |   |   | 6 |
| $3^\circ$ aluno |   | 2 | 5 |   |
| $4^\circ$ aluno |   |   |   |   |

Após algumas rodadas, a professora propõe os seguintes desafios:

a) Dada a sequência inicial $[1, 2, 4, 8]$, complete as sequências.

b) Crie uma sequência inicial que resulte em 5 sequências, com a última sendo o dígito 5.

c) Justifique por que não é possível obter 6 sequências, com a última sendo o dígito 5.

negatives.text:

III) O processo é repetido até que reste apenas um dígito.
IV) Se aparecer um zero, o processo é interrompido.

Após algumas rodadas, a professora propõe:

a) Dada a sequência inicial $[1, 2, 4, 8]$, complete as sequências.
