Let $O$ be the circumcenter of $\triangle ABC$, and let $H_{1}$ be the orthocenter of the triangle formed by the feet of the altitudes. Prove that the midpoint of segment $OH_{1}$ coincides with the incenter of the medial triangle of $\triangle A_{1}B_{1}C_{1}$.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be acute, with altitudes $AA_{1}$, $BB_{1}$, and $CC_{1}$ ($A_{1} \in BC$, $B_{1} \in CA$, $C_{1} \in AB$). Let $O$ be the circumcenter of $\triangle ABC$, and let $H_{1}$ be the orthocenter of $\triangle A_{1}B_{1}C_{1}$. Prove that the midpoint of segment $OH_{1}$ coincides with the centroid of the triangle with vertices at the midpoints of the sides of $\triangle A_{1}B_{1}C_{1}$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be acute, with altitudes $AA_{1}$, $BB_{1}$, and $CC_{1}$ ($A_{1} \in BC$, $B_{1} \in CA$, $C_{1} \in AB$). Let $O$ be the circumcenter of $\triangle ABC$, and let $H_{1}$ be the orthocenter of $\triangle A_{1}B_{1}C_{1}$. Prove that the midpoint of segment $OH_{1}$ coincides with the incenter of the triangle with vertices at the midpoints of the sides of $\triangle ABC$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be acute, with altitudes $AA_{1}$, $BB_{1}$, and $CC_{1}$ ($A_{1} \in BC$, $B_{1} \in CA$, $C_{1} \in AB$). Let $O$ be the circumcenter of $\triangle ABC$, and let $H_{1}$ be the centroid of $\triangle A_{1}B_{1}C_{1}$. Prove that the midpoint of segment $OH_{1}$ coincides with the incenter of the triangle with vertices at the midpoints of the sides of $\triangle A_{1}B_{1}C_{1}$.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ have an incircle tangent to $AC$ and $BC$ (with $AC \neq BC$) at points $P$ and $Q$, respectively. The $A$- and $B$-excircles are tangent to $AB$ at $M$ and $N$. Determine $\angle ACB$ if $M, N, P, Q$ lie on a circle.

negatives.text: The incircle of $\triangle ABC$ is tangent to $AC$ and $BC$ at $P$ and $Q$, respectively. The excircles to the sides $AC$ and $BC$ are tangent to the line $AB$ at points $M$ and $N$. Find $\angle ACB$ if the points $M, N, P$ and $Q$ are collinear.

The incircle of $\triangle ABC$ is tangent to $AC$ and $BC$ at $P$ and $Q$, respectively. The excircles to the sides $AC$ and $BC$ are tangent to the line $AB$ at points $M$ and $N$. Find $\angle ACB$ if the points $M, N, P$ and $Q$ lie on a parabola.

The incircle of $\triangle ABC$ is tangent to $AC$ and $BC$ at $P$ and $Q$, respectively. The excircles to the sides $AC$ and $BC$ are tangent to the line $AB$ at points $M$ and $N$. Find $\angle ACB$ if the points $M, N, P$ and $Q$ lie on a circle with center at $C$.

positive_text:
Let $\omega$ be the incircle of $\triangle ABC$ with $AC \neq BC$, and let $I$ be the incenter. Let $D$, $E$, and $F$ be the points of tangency of $\omega$ with sides $AB$, $BC$, and $AC$, respectively.

a) If $S = CI \cap EF$, prove that $\triangle CDI \sim \triangle DSI$.

b) Let $M$ be the second point of intersection of $CD$ with $\omega$. The tangent to $\omega$ at $M$ meets $AB$ at $G$. Prove that $GS \perp CI$.

negatives.text:
Let $k$ be the incircle of $\triangle ABC$ with $AC = BC$, $I$ be the center of $k$, and let $D$, $E$, and $F$ be the points of tangency with $AB$, $BC$, and $AC$, respectively.

a) Let $S = CI \cap EF$. Prove that $\triangle CDI \sim \triangle DSI$.

b) Let $M$ be the second point of intersection of $CD$ with $k$. The tangent to $k$ at $M$ intersects $AB$ at $G$. Prove that $GS \perp CI$.

Let $k$ be the incircle of $\triangle ABC$ with $AC \neq BC$, $I$ be the center of $k$, and let $D$, $E$, and $F$ be the points of tangency with $AB$, $BC$, and $AC$, respectively.

a) If $S = CI \cap EF$, prove that $\triangle CDI \sim \triangle DIF$.

b) Let $M$ be the second point of intersection of $CD$ with $k$. The tangent to $k$ at $M$ intersects $AB$ at $G$. Prove that $GS \perp CI$.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ have orthocenter $H$, and let $M$ denote the midpoint of $AB$. Let $H_1$ and $H_2$ be the projections of $H$ onto the internal and external angle bisectors of $\angle C$, respectively. Show that $H_1$, $H_2$, and $M$ lie on a straight line.

negatives.text: Let $H$ be the orthocenter of $\triangle ABC$, $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$ and $H_1$ and $H_2$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $H$ to the internal and external bisector of $\angle CAB$, respectively. Prove that the points $H_1$, $H_2$ and $M$ are colinear.

Let $H$ be the orthocenter of $\triangle ABC$, $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$ and $H_1$ and $H_2$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $H$ to the internal and external bisector of $\angle C$, respectively. Prove that the points $H_1$, $H_2$ and $M$ are concyclic.

Let $H$ be the orthocenter of $\triangle ABC$, $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$ and $H_1$ and $H_2$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $H$ to the internal and external bisector of $\angle C$, respectively. Prove that the points $H_1$, $H_2$ and $M$ are colinear if $\angle C$ is acute.

positive_text: Show that in any set of 9 vertices of a regular 26-gon, there exist three that form an isosceles triangle. Is it possible to choose 8 vertices such that no subset of three forms an isosceles triangle?

negatives.text: Prove that amongst any 9 vertices of a regular 26-gon there are three which are vertices of an equilateral triangle. Do there exist 8 vertices such that no three of them are vertices of an equilateral triangle?

Prove that amongst any 9 vertices of a regular 25-gon there are three which are vertices of an isosceles triangle. Do there exist 8 vertices such that no three of them are vertices of an isosceles triangle?

Prove that amongst any 8 vertices of a regular 26-gon there are three which are vertices of an isosceles triangle. Do there exist 7 vertices such that no three of them are vertices of an isosceles triangle?

positive_text: Let two tangent circles with centers $A$ and $B$ be inscribed in an angle. Prove that any circle centered on the segment $AB$, also inscribed in the angle, which goes through $A$ must also go through $B$.

negatives.text: Two tangent circles with centers $O_{1}$ and $O_{2}$ are inscribed in a given angle. Prove that if a third circle with center on the segment $O_{1}O_{2}$ is tangent to one of the sides of the angle and passes through one of the points $O_{1}$ and $O_{2}$, then it passes through the other.

Two tangent circles with centers $O_{1}$ and $O_{2}$ are inscribed in a given angle. Prove that if a third circle with center on the segment $O_{1}O_{2}$ is inscribed in the angle and is externally tangent to one of the points $O_{1}$ and $O_{2}$, then it is externally tangent to the other as well.

positive_text: In a game involving 5 participants, a set of 25 people all wish to participate. Determine the largest number of distinct games that can be formed, ensuring that no pair of individuals appears in more than one game together.

negatives.text: A card game is played by five persons. In a group of 25 persons all like to play that game. Find the maximum possible number of games which can be played if no player is allowed to play more than once.

A card game is played by five persons. In a group of 25 persons all like to play that game. Find the maximum possible number of games which can be played if no two players are allowed to play simultaneously more than twice.

A card game is played by five persons. In a group of 25 persons all like to play that game. Find the maximum possible number of games which can be played if no two players are allowed to play simultaneously more than once, and each player can participate in at most 3 games.

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, suppose $BL$ is the angle bisector of $\angle ABC$ with $L \in AC$ and $AH$ is the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$, with foot $H$. Show that $\angle AHL = \angle ALB$ is equivalent to the condition $\angle BAC = \angle ACB + 90^\circ$.

negatives.text: Let $BL$ be the angle bisector of $\angle ABC$ in triangle $ABC$ with $L$ on $AC$, and $AH$ the altitude from $A$ to $BC$. Prove that $\angle AHL = \angle ALB$ if and only if $\angle BAC = \angle ACB$.

positive_text:
Some cells in an $8 \times 8$ grid are marked with tokens satisfying the following conditions:

(i) Every rectangle of size $2 \times 1$ or $1 \times 2$ contains at least one token;

(ii) In every rectangle of size $7 \times 1$ or $1 \times 7$, there are two adjacent tokens.

Determine the smallest number of tokens needed to satisfy both conditions.

negatives.text:
Tokens are placed in some of the cells of a table of size $8 \times 8$ such that:

(1) there is at least one token in any rectangle of size $2 \times 1$ and $1 \times 2$;

(2) there are at least three tokens in any rectangle of size $7 \times 1$ and $1 \times 7$.

Find the minimum possible number of tokens.

Tokens are placed in some of the cells of a table of size $8 \times 8$ such that:

(1) there is at least one token in any rectangle of size $2 \times 1$ and $1 \times 2$;

(2) there are two non-neighboring tokens in any rectangle of size $7 \times 1$ and $1 \times 7$.

Find the minimum possible number of tokens.

positive_text: Can there be two triangles such that the measures of their angles, when arranged in some order, form an arithmetic sequence with a non-zero common difference?

negatives.text: Are there two triangles whose angles (in some order) form a geometric progression with a non-zero common ratio?
Are there two triangles whose angles (in some order) form an arithmetic progression with a zero common difference?
Are there two triangles whose angles (in some order) form an arithmetic progression with a negative common difference?

positive_text: A plane cuts a tetrahedron $ABCD$ and intersects the medians of triangles $DAB$, $DBC$, and $DCA$ from vertex $D$ in the proportions $1:2$, $1:3$, and $1:4$ respectively. Determine the ratio of the volumes of the two regions formed by the plane within the tetrahedron.

negatives.text: A plane intersects a tetrahedron $ABCD$ and divides the medians of the triangles $DAB$, $DBC$, and $DCA$ through $D$ in ratios $2:1$, $1:3$, and $1:4$ from $D$, respectively. Find the ratio of the volumes of the two parts of the tetrahedron cut by the plane.

A plane intersects a tetrahedron $ABCD$ and divides the medians of the triangles $DAB$, $DBC$, and $DCA$ through $D$ in ratios $1:2$, $1:3$, and $1:4$ from $D$, respectively. Find the ratio of the surface areas of the two parts of the tetrahedron cut by the plane.

A plane intersects a tetrahedron $ABCD$ and divides the medians of the triangles $DAB$, $DBC$, and $DCA$ through $D$ in ratios $1:2$, $1:3$, and $1:4$ from $D$, respectively. Find the ratio of the lengths of the two segments formed by the plane within the tetrahedron.

positive_text: In a game between Ivan and Peter, Ivan secretly selects a number from the set $A=\{1,2,\ldots,90\}$. Peter then chooses a subset $B$ of $A$, and Ivan replies whether the selected number is in $B$. If it is, Peter pays Ivan 2 leva; if not, he pays 1 lev. What is the minimal total amount Peter must be prepared to pay to guarantee identification of Ivan's number?

negatives.text: Ivan selects a number from the set $\{1,2,\ldots,90\}$. Peter chooses subsets $B$ of the set and Ivan replies whether the number is in $B$. Peter pays Ivan 2 leva for a "yes" and 0 leva for a "no". What is the minimal total payment Peter must make to guarantee finding Ivan's number?

Ivan selects a number from the set $\{1,2,\ldots,90\}$. Peter chooses subsets $B$ of the set and Ivan replies whether the number is in $B$. Peter pays Ivan 2 leva for a "yes" and 1 lev for a "no", but he can only make up to 5 queries. What is the minimal total payment Peter must make to guarantee finding Ivan's number?

positive_text: In a right triangle $ABC$ with $\angle ACB = 90^\circ$, let $CH$ be the altitude from $C$ to hypotenuse $AB$ with foot at $H$. Let the incircle of $\triangle ABC$ touch $AC$ at $P$ and $BC$ at $Q$. If the segment $AQ$ is perpendicular to $HP$, determine $\frac{AH}{BH}$.

negatives.text: Given a right triangle $ABC$ ($\angle ACB = 90^\circ$), let $CH$, $H \in AB$, be the altitude to $AB$ and $P$ and $Q$ be the tangent points of the incircle of $\triangle ABC$ to $AC$ and $BC$, respectively. If $AQ \perp HP$, find the ratio $\frac{AH}{BH} + 1$.

positive_text: Let a unit cube be given. A plane is defined to pass through one vertex of the bottom face and the centers of the two adjacent vertical faces that do not include the vertex. Determine the ratio of the volumes of the two regions formed by the plane slicing the cube.

negatives.text: A plane passes through a vertex of the base of a cube of edge $1$ and the centers of its two faces that contain that vertex. Find the ratio of the volumes of the two parts of the cube cut by the plane.

A plane passes through a vertex of the base of a cube of edge $1$ and the centers of its two adjacent vertical faces. Find the ratio of the surface areas of the two parts of the cube cut by the plane.

positive_text: In a beach volleyball tournament with $n$ players and $n$ matches, every pair of players plays together in at least one match. What is the largest possible value of $n$?

negatives.text: In a beach volleyball tournament with $n$ players and $n$ matches, any two players play in one and the same match at most once. Find the maximal value of $n$.
In a beach volleyball tournament with $n$ players and $n$ matches, any two players play in one and the same match exactly once. Find the maximal value of $n$.
In a beach volleyball tournament with $n$ players and $n$ matches, any three players play in one and the same match at least once. Find the maximal value of $n$.

positive_text: Given a regular heptagon $A_1A_2A_3A_4A_5A_6A_7$, with sides $A_iA_{i+1}$ opposite to vertex $A_{i+3}$ (indices modulo 7). Let $P$ be any interior point of the heptagon. A line from $P$ to a vertex $A_i$ is said to intersect the boundary at a good point if the intersection lies in the interior of the side opposite to $A_i$. Show that for any such point $P$, the number of good points is odd.

negatives.text: A regular heptagon $ABCDEFG$ is given. The sides $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DE$, $EF$, $FG$, and $GA$ are opposite to the vertices $E$, $F$, $G$, $A$, $B$, $C$, and $D$, respectively. If $M$ is an interior point, a line through $M$ and a vertex intersects the boundary at a good point if the intersection lies on the side opposite to the vertex. Prove that for every point $M$, the number of good points is even.

A regular heptagon $ABCDEFG$ is given. The sides $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DE$, $EF$, $FG$, and $GA$ are opposite to the vertices $E$, $F$, $G$, $A$, $B$, $C$, and $D$, respectively. If $M$ is an interior point, a line through $M$ and a vertex intersects the boundary at a good point if the intersection lies on the side opposite to the vertex. Prove that for every point $M$, the number of good points is at least 3.

positive_text: A country has $n$ cities, and each pair is connected by a single one-way or two-way road. Suppose that for every subset of $k$ cities, there exists a cyclic path that visits each city exactly once. What is the maximum number of one-way roads the country can have?

negatives.text: Every two of $n$ towns in a country are connected by one way or two way road. It is known that for every $k$ towns there exists a path (not necessarily cyclic) passing through each of these $k$ towns exactly once. Find the maximal possible number of one way roads.

Every two of $n$ towns in a country are connected by one way or two way road. It is known that for every $k$ towns there exists a round trip passing through each of these $k$ towns at most once. Find the maximal possible number of one way roads.

Every two of $n$ towns in a country are connected by one way or two way road. It is known that for every $k$ towns there exists a round trip passing through each of these $k$ towns at least once. Find the maximal possible number of one way roads.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ have incircle $k$ tangent to $BC$ and $CA$ at $P$ and $Q$, respectively. Let $J$ be the excenter opposite to $AB$ in $\angle ABC$, and define $T$ as the second intersection point of the circumcircles of $\angle JBP$ and $\angle JAQ$. Prove that the circumcircle of $\angle ABT$ is tangent to $k$.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ have incircle $k$ tangent to $BC$ and $CA$ at $P$ and $Q$, respectively. Let $J$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$, and define $T$ as the second intersection point of the circumcircles of $\angle JBP$ and $\angle JAQ$. Prove that the circumcircle of $\angle ABT$ touches $k$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ have incircle $k$ tangent to $BC$ and $CA$ at $P$ and $Q$, respectively. Let $J$ be the excenter opposite to $AB$ in $\angle ABC$, and define $T$ as the second intersection point of the circumcircles of $\angle JBP$ and $\angle JBQ$. Prove that the circumcircle of $\angle ABT$ touches $k$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ have incircle $k$ tangent to $BC$ and $CA$ at $P$ and $Q$, respectively. Let $J$ be the excenter opposite to $AB$ in $\angle ABC$, and define $T$ as the second intersection point of the circumcircles of $\angle JCP$ and $\angle JAQ$. Prove that the circumcircle of $\angle ABT$ touches $k$.

positive_text: Prove that, for all positive real numbers $x$, $y$, $z$, and $w$, the following inequality holds: $$\sum_{cyc} \frac{x^4}{x^3 + x^2 y + x y^2 + y^3} \ge \frac{x + y + z + w}{4}.$$

negatives.text: Show that, for all positive real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$, and $d$, the following inequality holds: $$\sum_{cyc} \frac{a^4}{a^3 - a^2 b - ab^2 + b^3} \ge \frac{a+b+c+d}{4}.$$
Show that, for all positive real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$, and $d$, the following inequality holds: $$\sum_{cyc} \frac{a^3}{a^3 + a^2 b + ab^2 + b^3} \ge \frac{a+b+c+d}{4}.$$
Show that, for all positive real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$, and $d$, the following inequality holds: $$\sum_{cyc} \frac{a^4}{a^3 + a^2 b + ab^2 + b^3} \le \frac{a+b+c+d}{4}.$$

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral inscribed in a circle $k$. Let $AC$ and $BD$ intersect at $E$, and $AD$ and $BC$ intersect at $F$. Prove that the line joining the incenters of $\triangle ABE$ and $\triangle ABF$ and the line joining the incenters of $\triangle CDE$ and $\triangle CDF$ intersect on $k$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be cyclic with circumcircle $k$. If $AC$ and $BD$ intersect at $E$, and $AD$ and $BC$ intersect at $F$, prove that the line through the incenters of $\triangle ABE$ and $\triangle ABD$ and the line through the incenters of $\triangle CDE$ and $\triangle CDF$ intersect on $k$.

Let $ABCD$ be cyclic with circumcircle $k$. If $AC$ and $BD$ intersect at $E$, and $AD$ and $BC$ intersect at $F$, prove that the line through the incenters of $\triangle ABE$ and $\triangle ABF$ and the line through the incenters of $\triangle CDE$ and $\triangle CDF$ intersect at a point inside $k$.

Let $ABCD$ be cyclic with circumcircle $k$. If $AC$ and $BD$ intersect at $E$, and $AD$ and $BC$ intersect at $F$, prove that the line through the incenters of $\triangle ABE$ and $\triangle ABF$ and the line through the incenters of $\triangle CDE$ and $\triangle CDF$ intersect on a different circle $k'$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with non-parallel sides $AB$ and $CD$. Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of segments $AD$ and $BC$, respectively. If the line $MN$ intersects the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ at $K$ and $L$, show that the circumcircles of $\triangle AKM$ and $\triangle BNL$ intersect at a point lying on the segment $AB$.

negatives.text: In quadrilateral $ABCD$, sides $AB$ and $CD$ are not parallel. Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of $AD$ and $BC$, respectively. The line $MN$ intersects the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ at $K$ and $L$. Prove that the circumcircles of triangles $AKM$ and $BNL$ intersect on the line $CD$.

In quadrilateral $ABCD$, sides $AB$ and $CD$ are not parallel. Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of $AD$ and $BC$, respectively. The line $MN$ intersects the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ at $K$ and $L$. Prove that the circumcircles of triangles $AKM$ and $BNL$ intersect on the line $CD$.

In quadrilateral $ABCD$, sides $AB$ and $CD$ are not parallel. Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of $AD$ and $BC$, respectively. The line $MN$ intersects the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ at $K$ and $L$. Prove that the circumcircles of triangles $AKM$ and $BNL$ intersect at a point not lying on the line $AB$.

positive_text: \text{Find all } x > 0 \text{ such that } (x+1)\log_3 x + 4x \log_3 x = 16.

negatives.text: \text{Solve } (x+1)\log_3 x - 4x \log_3 x - 16 = 0.
\text{Solve } (x+1)\log_3 x + 4x \log_3 x^2 - 16 = 0.
\text{Solve } (x+1)\log_3 x + 4x \log_3 x = -16.

positive_text: Inspector Goodenough is investigating a theft of Lady Gilmore's pearl necklace. Seven servants—$A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, $F$, $G$—entered the room containing the necklace. Each claimed to have been there only once. They also claimed the following meetings: $A$ met $B$, $C$, $F$, $G$; $B$ met $A$, $C$, $D$, $E$, $F$; $C$ met $A$, $B$, $E$; $E$ met $B$, $C$, $F$; $F$ met $A$, $B$, $D$, $E$; $G$ met $A$, $D$; and $D$ met $B$, $F$, $G$. If one of them is lying, who is it?

negatives.text: Seven individuals—$A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, $F$, $G$—entered a room. Each claimed to have entered only once. They stated the following meetings: $A$ met $B$, $C$, $F$, $G$; $B$ met $A$, $C$, $D$, $E$, $F$; $C$ met $A$, $B$, $E$; $E$ met $B$, $C$, $F$; $F$ met $A$, $B$, $D$, $E$; $G$ met $A$, $D$; and $D$ met $B$, $F$, $G$. However, one of them is telling the truth about not meeting someone they said they did. Who is the one being truthful about not meeting someone?

Seven individuals—$A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, $F$, $G$—entered a room. Each claimed to have entered only once. They stated the following meetings: $A$ met $B$, $C$, $F$, $G$; $B$ met $A$, $C$, $D$, $E$, $F$; $C$ met $A$, $B$, $E$; $E$ met $B$, $C$, $F$; $F$ met $A$, $B$, $D$, $E$; $G$ met $A$, $D$; and $D$ met $B$, $F$, $G$. It is known that two of them are lying. Who are the two?

Seven individuals—$A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, $F$, $G$—entered a room. Each claimed to have entered only once. They stated the following meetings: $A$ met $B$, $C$, $F$, $G$; $B$ met $A$, $C$, $D$, $E$, $F$; $C$ met $A$, $B$, $E$; $E$ met $B$, $C$, $F$; $F$ met $A$, $B$, $D$, $E$; $G$ met $A$, $D$; and $D$ met $B$, $F$, $G$. It is known that one of them is lying, and that the person who lied never met anyone in the room. Who is the liar?

positive_text: Determine all positive integers $ k $ such that there exist positive integers $ x, y $ with $ y > x $ for which $ \frac{x^k y}{y^2 - x^2} $ is a prime number.

negatives.text: Find all natural numbers $ k $ for which there exist natural numbers $ x, y $ such that the number $ \frac{x^k y}{y^2 + x^2} $ is prime.
Find all natural numbers $ k $ for which there exist natural numbers $ x, y $ such that the number $ \frac{x^k y}{y^2 - x^2} $ is composite.

positive_text: Given 11 equally spaced points on a circle, suppose that some chords are drawn and each is colored either red or blue. If no two chords of the same color intersect at an interior point, what is the maximum number of chords that can be drawn?

negatives.text: Given 11 points equally spaced on a circle, suppose that some chords are drawn and colored with two colors. If each chord intersects at most one other chord of the opposite color, what is the maximum number of chords that can be drawn?

There are 11 points equally spaced on a circle. Suppose some chords are drawn and colored in two colors, such that no two chords of the same color are tangent. What is the maximum number of chords that can be drawn?

Given 11 points equally spaced on a circle, suppose that some chords are drawn and colored in two colors, so that each chord meets at most one other chord from the same color at an endpoint. What is the maximum number of chords that can be drawn?

positive_text: Given is a convex polygon $P$ with 2024 vertices $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_{2024}$ and 1000 interior points with no three collinear. The polygon is triangulated by connecting some of these interior points. Each vertex is labeled with a number from the set $\{1, -1, 2, -2\}$ such that for every $i = 1, 2, \dots, 1012$, the labels of $A_i$ and $A_{i+1012}$ are additive inverses. Prove that at least one triangle in the triangulation has two vertices with labels summing to zero.

negatives.text: Given is a convex 2024-gon $A_1A_2\dots A_{2024}$ and 1000 points inside it, no three collinear. The polygon is triangulated. Each point is assigned a number from $\{1, -1, 2, -2\}$, with the condition that the sum of the numbers at $A_i$ and $A_{i+1012}$ is positive for all $i = 1, 2, \dots, 1012$. Prove that there is a triangle such that the sum of the numbers in some two of its vertices is positive.

Given is a convex 2024-gon $A_1A_2\dots A_{2024}$ and 1000 points inside it, no three collinear. The polygon is triangulated. Each point is assigned a number from $\{1, -1, 2, -2\}$, with the condition that the sum of the numbers at $A_i$ and $A_{i+1012}$ is positive for all $i = 1, 2, \dots, 1012$. Prove that there is a triangle such that the sum of the numbers in all three of its vertices is positive.

Given is a convex 2024-gon $A_1A_2\dots A_{2024}$ and 1000 points inside it, no three collinear. The polygon is triangulated. Each point is assigned a number from $\{1, -1, 2, -2\}$, with the condition that the product of the numbers at $A_i$ and $A_{i+1012}$ is negative for all $i = 1, 2, \dots, 1012$. Prove that there is a triangle such that the product of the numbers in some two of its vertices is negative.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be a right-angled isosceles triangle with legs of unit length. Let $P$ lie on the hypotenuse, and let $Q$ and $R$ be the projections of $P$ onto $AB$ and $AC$, respectively. Denote the areas of triangles $APQ$ and $PBR$, as well as the area of the rectangle $QCRP$. Show that, for any position of $P$, the maximum among these three areas is at least $\frac{2}{9}$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a right-angled isosceles triangle with legs of length $1$. Let $P$ lie on the hypotenuse, and let $Q$ and $R$ be the projections of $P$ onto $AB$ and $AC$, respectively. Consider the areas of triangles $APQ$ and $PBR$, and the area of the rectangle $QCRP$. Prove that the smallest of these three areas is at least $\frac{2}{9}$.

Let $ABC$ be a right-angled isosceles triangle with legs of length $1$. Let $P$ lie on the hypotenuse, and let $Q$ and $R$ be the projections of $P$ onto $AB$ and $AC$, respectively. Consider the areas of triangles $APQ$ and $PBR$, and the area of the rectangle $QCRP$. Prove that the sum of these three areas is at least $\frac{2}{9}$.

Let $ABC$ be a right-angled isosceles triangle with legs of length $1$. Let $P$ lie on the hypotenuse, and let $Q$ and $R$ be the projections of $P$ onto $AB$ and $AC$, respectively. Consider the areas of triangles $APQ$ and $PBR$, and the area of the rectangle $QCRP$. Prove that the largest of these three areas is at least $\frac{1}{4}$.

positive_text: Construct a quadrilateral $PQRS$ with: (i) the measures of the four sides $PQ$, $QR$, $RS$, and $SP$; (ii) the condition that $PQ$ is parallel to $RS$; (iii) the sides $QR$ and $SP$ do not cross.

negatives.text: Describe a construction of a quadrilateral $ABCD$ given: (i) the lengths of all four sides; (ii) that $AB$ and $CD$ are perpendicular; (iii) that $BC$ and $DA$ do not intersect.
Describe a construction of a quadrilateral $ABCD$ given: (i) the lengths of all four sides; (ii) that $AB$ and $CD$ are parallel; (iii) that $BC$ and $DA$ intersect.
Describe a construction of a quadrilateral $ABCD$ given: (i) the lengths of all four sides; (ii) that $AB$ and $CD$ are not parallel; (iii) that $BC$ and $DA$ do not intersect.

positive_text:
Let $h(n)$ be the $n$th harmonic number defined as $h(n) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{1}{k}$. Show that for all integers $n \geq 2$,
$$
\sum_{k=1}^{n-1} h(k) + n = n h(n)
$$

negatives.text:
Let $h(n) = 1 + \frac{1}{2} + \cdots + \frac{1}{n}$. Prove that for $n \geq 2$,
$$
\sum_{k=1}^{n-1} h(k) + n = n h(n) + 1
$$

Let $h(n) = 1 + \frac{1}{2} + \cdots + \frac{1}{n}$. Prove that for $n \geq 2$,
$$
\sum_{k=1}^{n-1} h(k) + n = n h(n - 1)
$$

Let $h(n) = 1 + \frac{1}{2} + \cdots + \frac{1}{n}$. Prove that for $n \geq 2$,
$$
\sum_{k=1}^{n-1} h(k) + n = n h(n)^2
$$

positive_text: Suppose you have four weights arranged in a geometric sequence and an equal arm balance. Devise a strategy to identify the heaviest weight using the balance only twice.

negatives.text: Given four weights in arithmetic progression and an equal arm balance, show how to find the heaviest weight using the balance only twice.
Given four weights in geometric progression and a digital scale, show how to find the heaviest weight using the scale only twice.

positive_text: A right circular cone has a base with radius $1$ cm and a slant height of $3$ cm. Let $P$ be a point on the boundary of the base. The shortest path on the surface of the cone from $P$ that goes all the way around and returns to $P$ is constructed. Determine the smallest possible distance from the apex $V$ to this path.

negatives.text: A right circular cone of base radius $1$ cm and slant height $3$ cm is given. $P$ is a point on the circumference of the base and a path from $P$ around the cone and back to $P$ is drawn, but it is not necessarily the shortest such path. What is the minimum distance from the vertex $V$ to this path?

A right circular cone of base radius $1$ cm and slant height $3$ cm is given. $P$ is a point on the circumference of the base and the longest path from $P$ around the cone and back to $P$ is drawn. What is the minimum distance from the vertex $V$ to this path?

A right circular cone of base radius $1$ cm and slant height $3$ cm is given. $P$ is a point on the circumference of the base and the shortest path from $P$ around the cone and back to $P$ is drawn. What is the maximum distance from the vertex $V$ to this path?

positive_text: Suppose $n$ is an integer such that the second digit from the right in $n^2$ is $7$. Determine the last digit of $n^2$.

negatives.text: Let $n$ be an integer. If the tens digit of $n^2$ is $7$, what is the hundreds digit of $n^2$?
Let $n$ be an integer. If the units digit of $n^2$ is $7$, what is the tens digit of $n^2$?
Let $n$ be an integer. If the tens digit of $n^2$ is $7$, what is the units digit of $n$?

positive_text: Define a positive integer as digitally divisible if it contains no digit equal to zero and is divisible by the sum of its digits. Prove that there exist infinitely many such integers.

negatives.text: An integer is digitally divisible if none of its digits is zero and the sum of its digits divides the integer. Show that there are only finitely many digitally divisible integers.
An integer is digitally divisible if all its digits are non-zero and it is divisible by the product of its digits. Show that there are infinitely many digitally divisible integers.
An integer is digitally divisible if it contains at least one zero digit and is divisible by the sum of its digits. Show that there are infinitely many digitally divisible integers.

positive_text: Given an acute triangle with area 1, prove that there exists a point within the triangle such that the distance from this point to each of the triangle's vertices is no less than $\frac{2}{\sqrt[4]{27}}$.

negatives.text: An acute-angled triangle has unit area. Show that there is a point inside the triangle whose distance from each of the vertices is at most $\frac{2}{\sqrt[4]{27}}$.
An acute-angled triangle has unit area. Show that there is a point inside the triangle whose distance from each of the vertices is at least $\frac{2}{\sqrt{27}}$.
An acute-angled triangle has unit area. Show that there is a point outside the triangle whose distance from each of the vertices is at least $\frac{2}{\sqrt[4]{27}}$.

positive_text: Suppose line segments $AB = 1$ and $CD = 1$, with $\angle ABC = 90^\circ$ and $\angle CBD = 30^\circ$. Determine the length of segment $AC$.

negatives.text: Suppose $AB = 1$ and $CD = 1$, with $\angle ABC = 90^\circ$ and $\angle CBD = 60^\circ$. Find the length of $AC$.
Given $AB = 1$ and $CD = 2$, with $\angle ABC = 90^\circ$ and $\angle CBD = 30^\circ$, find the length of $AC$.
Let $AB = 1$ and $CD = 1$, with $\angle ABC = 90^\circ$ and $\angle CBD = 30^\circ$. Find the length of segment $AD$ instead of $AC$.

positive_text: Let $T_n$ be a triangular array with $\frac{1}{2} n(n+1)$ distinct real numbers placed randomly. For each row $k$, define $L_k$ to be the maximum number in row $k$. Determine the probability that $L_1 < L_2 < L_3 < \cdots < L_n$.

negatives.text: A set of $\frac{1}{2} n(n+1)$ distinct numbers is arranged at random in a triangular array. Let $M_k$ be the largest number in the $k$-th row from the top. Find the probability that $M_{1} \leq M_{2} \leq M_{3} \leq \cdots \leq M_{n}$.

A set of $\frac{1}{2} n(n+1)$ distinct numbers is arranged at random in a triangular array. Let $M_k$ be the smallest number in the $k$-th row from the top. Find the probability that $M_{1} < M_{2} < M_{3} < \cdots < M_{n}$.

A set of $\frac{1}{2} n(n+1)$ distinct numbers is arranged at random in a triangular array. Let $M_k$ be the second largest number in the $k$-th row from the top. Find the probability that $M_{1} < M_{2} < M_{3} < \cdots < M_{n}$.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be acute, with $D$ the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$. Let $H$ be an arbitrary point on segment $AD$. If $BH$ meets $AC$ at $E$ and $CH$ meets $AB$ at $F$, show that $\angle EDH = \angle FDH$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AD$ the altitude on $BC$. Let $H$ be any point on $AD$. Lines $BH$ and $CH$ intersect $AC$ and $AB$ at $E$ and $F$, respectively. Prove that $\angle EDF = \angle FDH$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AD$ the altitude on $BC$. Let $H$ be any point on segment $AD$. Lines $BH$ and $CH$ intersect $AC$ and $AB$ at $E$ and $F$, respectively. Prove that $\angle EDH + \angle FDH = 90^\circ$.

positive_text: On a standard 12-hour analog clock, the hour and minute hands move continuously. Suppose $m$ is an integer such that $1 \leq m \leq 720$. If the angle between the hour and minute hands is exactly $1^\circ$ at $m$ minutes after 12:00, find all such values of $m$.

negatives.text: On a standard 12-hour clock, the hour and minute hands move continuously. Let $m$ be an integer such that $1 \leq m \leq 720$. At $m$ minutes after 12:00, the angle between the hour and minute hands is exactly $1^\circ$ only if $m$ is even. Determine all such values of $m$.

positive_text: \begin{gathered}a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}=a+b+c, \text{ and } \\a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}=a b c.\end{gathered}

negatives.text: \begin{gathered}x^{3}+y^{3}+z^{3}=x+y+z, \text{ and } \\x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2} = -x y z.\end{gathered}
\begin{gathered}x^{3}+y^{3}+z^{3}=x+y+z, \text{ and } \\x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2} = x y z + 1.\end{gathered}
\begin{gathered}x^{3}+y^{3}+z^{3}=x+y+z, \text{ and } \\x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2} = x^{2} y z.\end{gathered}

positive_text:
Determine all ordered triples $(a, b, c)$ of real numbers such that:
$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
a b = c - a - b \\
a c = b - a - c \\
b c = a - b - c
\end{array}\right.
$$

negatives.text:
Find all ordered triples $(x, y, z)$ of real numbers satisfying:
$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
xy = z + x + y \\
xz = y + x + z \\
yz = x + y + z
\end{array}\right.
$$

Find all ordered triples $(x, y, z)$ of real numbers satisfying:
$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
xy = z - x - y \\
xz = y - x - z \\
yz = x - y - z
\end{array}\right.
$$ with the additional constraint that $x + y + z = 0$.

Find all ordered triples $(x, y, z)$ of real numbers satisfying:
$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
xy = z - x - y \\
xz = y - x - z \\
yz = x - y - z
\end{array}\right.
$$ with the equations replaced by their squares:
$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
(xy)^2 = (z - x - y)^2 \\
(xz)^2 = (y - x - z)^2 \\
(yz)^2 = (x - y - z)^2
\end{array}\right.
$$

positive_text: Derive a closed-form expression for the total number of $2 \times n$ black-and-white grids such that every black square has a white square either to its left in the same row or above it in the same column.

negatives.text: Find a closed formula for the number of $2 \times n$ grids where no black square is stranded, but now a black square is stranded if there is a black square to its left in the same row and a black square above it in the same column.
Find a closed formula for the number of $2 \times n$ grids with no stranded black squares, where a black square is stranded if it is the only black square in its row and column.

Find a closed formula for the number of $2 \times n$ grids with no stranded white squares, where a white square is stranded if it has a black square to its left in the same row and a black square above it in the same column.

positive_text: Robots are placed on the cells of a finite rectangular grid. Each edge (including those on the boundary) is labeled as *open* or *closed*. All boundary edges are *closed*. At each step, you can issue a direction (up, down, left, right), and every robot attempts to move in that direction. A robot moves only if the adjacent edge in the chosen direction is *open*. Suppose that for any robot and any target cell, there is a finite sequence of commands to move the robot to that cell. Prove that there exists a finite sequence of commands that will bring all robots to the same cell simultaneously.

negatives.text: Robots are placed on a finite rectangular grid. Each edge is either *passable* or *impassable*. The boundary edges are *impassable*. You can issue a sequence of movement commands. A robot moves in the direction of a command if the adjacent edge is *passable*. Suppose that for any robot and any target cell, there is a finite sequence of commands to move that robot to that cell. Prove that you can give a finite sequence of commands such that all robots end up on *distinct* cells at the same time.

Robots are placed on a finite rectangular grid. Each edge is either *passable* or *impassable*. The boundary edges are *impassable*. You can issue a sequence of movement commands. A robot moves in the direction of a command if the adjacent edge is *passable*. Suppose that for any robot and any target cell, there is a finite sequence of commands to move that robot to that cell. Prove that you can give a finite sequence of commands such that all robots end up on the same cell at the same time, and the number of commands is less than 100.

positive_text:
Let $x_1$, $x_2$, $\dots$, $x_n$ be positive real numbers with $x_1 x_2 \cdots x_n = 1$. Prove that
$$
\sum_{k=1}^n \frac{x_k}{\prod_{i=1}^k (1+x_i)}
$$
is at least $\frac{2^n - 1}{2^n}$.

negatives.text:
Let $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ be positive real numbers such that $\prod_{i=1}^n a_i = 1$. Show that
$$
\frac{a_1}{1+a_1} + \frac{a_2}{(1+a_1)(1+a_2)} + \cdots + \frac{a_n}{\prod_{i=1}^n (1+a_i)}
$$
is less than or equal to $\frac{2^n - 1}{2^n}$.

Let $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ be positive real numbers such that $\prod_{i=1}^n a_i = 2$. Show that
$$
\frac{a_1}{1+a_1} + \frac{a_2}{(1+a_1)(1+a_2)} + \cdots + \frac{a_n}{\prod_{i=1}^n (1+a_i)}
$$
is greater than or equal to $\frac{2^n - 1}{2^n}$.

Let $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ be positive real numbers such that $\prod_{i=1}^n a_i = 1$. Show that
$$
\frac{a_1^2}{1+a_1} + \frac{a_2^2}{(1+a_1)(1+a_2)} + \cdots + \frac{a_n^2}{\prod_{i=1}^n (1+a_i)}
$$
is greater than or equal to $\frac{2^n - 1}{2^n}$.

positive_text: In a class of 20 students, each student is connected to exactly three others via a mutual friendship. Initially, five students have concert tickets. A student will buy a ticket if at least two of their friends already have one. Can all 20 students end up with concert tickets?

negatives.text: There are 20 students in a class, each with exactly three close friends. Five students have bought tickets. A student will buy a ticket only if all three of their close friends have tickets. Is it possible for all 20 students to buy tickets?

There are 20 students in a class, each with exactly three close friends. Five students have bought tickets. A student will buy a ticket if at least one of their close friends has bought a ticket. Is it possible for all 20 students to buy tickets?

There are 20 students in a class, each with exactly three close friends. Five students have bought tickets. A student will buy a ticket if at least two of their close friends have NOT bought tickets. Is it possible for all 20 students to buy tickets?

positive_text: Let $ O $ be the circumcenter of an acute triangle $ \triangle ABC $, and suppose $ P $ lies within $ \triangle AOB $. Let the feet of perpendiculars from $ P $ to $ BC $, $ CA $, and $ AB $ be $ D $, $ E $, and $ F $ respectively. Show that the parallelogram constructed with vectors $ \vec{FE} $ and $ \vec{FD} $ lies entirely within $ \triangle ABC $.

negatives.text: Let $ O $ be the circumcenter of an acute triangle $ \triangle ABC $. Take a point $ P $ in the interior of $ \triangle AOB $, and let $ F $, $ E $, and $ D $ be the projections of $ P $ on $ AB $, $ AC $, and $ BC $, respectively. Prove that the parallelogram formed by segments $ FE $ and $ ED $ as adjacent sides lies entirely within $ \triangle ABC $.

Let $ O $ be the circumcenter of an acute triangle $ \triangle ABC $. Take a point $ P $ in the interior of $ \triangle AOB $, and let $ F $, $ E $, and $ D $ be the projections of $ P $ on $ AB $, $ AC $, and $ BC $, respectively. Prove that the parallelogram formed by segments $ FE $ and $ FD $ as adjacent sides lies entirely outside $ \triangle ABC $.

Let $ O $ be the circumcenter of an acute triangle $ \triangle ABC $. Take a point $ P $ in the interior of $ \triangle AOB $, and let $ F $, $ E $, and $ D $ be the projections of $ P $ on $ AB $, $ AC $, and $ BC $, respectively. Prove that the parallelogram formed by segments $ FE $ and $ FD $ as adjacent sides lies entirely within $ \triangle ABC $, even when $ P $ lies outside $ \triangle AOB $.

positive_text: Let $ S = (a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n) $ be a binary sequence of maximum length such that any two distinct substrings of five consecutive elements are unique. Show that the initial four elements of $ S $ are equal to the final four elements of $ S $.

negatives.text: Assume that $ S = (a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n) $ consists of $ 0 $ and $ 1 $ and is the longest sequence of numbers which satisfies the following condition: Every two sections of successive $ 5 $ terms in the sequence of numbers $ S $ are equal, i.e., for arbitrary $ 1 \leq i < j \leq n-4 $, $ (a_i, a_{i+1}, a_{i+2}, a_{i+3}, a_{i+4}) $ and $ (a_j, a_{j+1}, a_{j+2}, a_{j+3}, a_{j+4}) $ are equal. Prove that the first four terms and the last four terms in the sequence are the same.

Assume that $ S = (a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n) $ consists of $ 0 $ and $ 1 $ and is the longest sequence of numbers which satisfies the following condition: Every two sections of successive $ 5 $ terms in the sequence of numbers $ S $ are different, i.e., for arbitrary $ 1 \leq i < j \leq n-4 $, $ (a_i, a_{i+1}, a_{i+2}, a_{i+3}, a_{i+4}) $ and $ (a_j, a_{j+1}, a_{j+2}, a_{j+3}, a_{j+4}) $ are different. Prove that the first five terms and the last five terms in the sequence are the same.

positive_text: Assign the integers $1$ through $8$ to the eight vertices of a cube. Ensure that for every face, the sum of any three of its four vertex numbers is at least $10$. Determine the smallest possible total of the four numbers on a single face.

negatives.text: Put numbers $1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7$, and $8$ at the vertices of a cube, such that the sum of any three numbers on any face is not greater than $10$. Find the maximum sum of the four numbers on a face.
Put numbers $1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7$, and $8$ at the vertices of a cube, such that the sum of any two numbers on any face is not less than $10$. Find the minimum sum of the four numbers on a face.
Put numbers $1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7$, and $8$ at the vertices of a cube, such that the sum of any three numbers on any face is not less than $10$. Find the minimum product of the four numbers on a face.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be acute with incenter $I$ and orthocenter $H$. Let $B_1$ and $C_1$ be the midpoints of $AC$ and $AB$ respectively. If ray $B_1I$ meets $AB$ at $B_2$ ($B_2 \neq B$) and ray $C_1I$ meets the extension of $AC$ at $C_2$, and if $B_2C_2$ intersects $BC$ at $K$, let $A_1$ be the circumcenter of $\triangle BHC$. Prove that points $A$, $I$, and $A_1$ are collinear if and only if the areas of $\triangle BKB_2$ and $\triangle CKC_2$ are equal.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ be acute with incenter $I$ and orthocenter $H$. Let $B_1$ and $C_1$ be the midpoints of $AC$ and $AB$, respectively. Suppose ray $B_1I$ intersects $AB$ at $B_2$ ($B_2 \neq B$), and ray $C_1I$ intersects the extension of $AC$ at $C_2$. If the segment $B_2C_2$ intersects $BC$ at $K$, and $A_1$ is the circumcenter of triangle $BHC$, prove that the collinearity of $A$, $I$, and $A_1$ is equivalent to the inequality of the areas of $\triangle BKB_2$ and $\triangle CKC_2$.

Let triangle $ABC$ be acute with incenter $I$ and orthocenter $H$. Let $B_1$ and $C_1$ be the midpoints of $AC$ and $AB$, respectively. Suppose ray $B_1I$ intersects $AB$ at $B_2$ ($B_2 \neq B$), and ray $C_1I$ intersects the extension of $AC$ at $C_2$. If the segment $B_2C_2$ intersects $BC$ at $K$, and $A_1$ is the circumcenter of triangle $BHC$, prove that the collinearity of $A$, $I$, and $A_1$ is equivalent to the sum of the areas of $\triangle BKB_2$ and $\triangle CKC_2$ being equal to a fixed constant.

Let triangle $ABC$ be acute with incenter $I$ and orthocenter $H$. Let $B_1$ and $C_1$ be the midpoints of $AC$ and $AB$, respectively. Suppose ray $B_1I$ intersects $AB$ at $B_2$ ($B_2 \neq B$), and ray $C_1I$ intersects the extension of $AC$ at $C_2$. If the segment $B_2C_2$ intersects $BC$ at $K$, and $A_1$ is the circumcenter of triangle $BHC$, prove that the collinearity of $A$, $I$, and $A_1$ is equivalent to the sum of the perimeters of $\triangle BKB_2$ and $\triangle CKC_2$ being equal.

positive_text:
In a coordinate system $xOy$, let $A(0, \frac{4}{3})$, $B(-1, 0)$, and $C(1, 0)$. For any point $P$, the distance from $P$ to the line $BC$ equals the square root of the product of the distances from $P$ to lines $AB$ and $AC$.

(1) Determine the equation of the locus of point $P$.

(2) If a line $L$ passes through the incenter $D$ of triangle $ABC$, and intersects the locus of $P$ at exactly 3 points, find all possible slopes $k$ of such a line $L$.

negatives.text:
In a plane rectangular coordinate system $xOy$, let $A(0, \frac{4}{3})$, $B(-1, 0)$, and $C(1, 0)$. The distance from point $P$ to line $BC$ is the arithmetic mean of the distances from $P$ to lines $AB$ and $AC$.

(1) Find the locus equation of point $P$.

(2) If line $L$ passes through the incenter $D$ of $\triangle ABC$, and has exactly 3 common points with the locus of $P$, find all values of the slope $k$ of line $L$.

In a plane rectangular coordinate system $xOy$, let $A(0, \frac{4}{3})$, $B(-1, 0)$, and $C(1, 0)$. The distance from point $P$ to line $BC$ is the harmonic mean of the distances from $P$ to lines $AB$ and $AC$.

(1) Find the equation of the locus of point $P$.

(2) If line $L$ passes through the incenter $D$ of $\triangle ABC$, and has exactly 3 common points with the locus of $P$, find all values of the slope $k$ of line $L$.

positive_text:
Let $P$ be a set of $n$ points in the plane, such that:
(1) there are 7 points in $P$ that form the vertices of a convex 7-gon;
(2) for every convex pentagon formed by 5 points in $P$, there exists at least one point of $P$ inside that pentagon.

Determine the smallest possible value of $n$.

negatives.text:
Let $M$ be a set of $n$ points in the plane such that:
(1) there exist 7 points in $M$ which form a convex heptagon;
(2) if for any 5 points in $M$ that form a convex pentagon, there is a point in $M$ that lies on the boundary of the pentagon.

Find the minimum value of $n$.

Let $M$ be a set of $n$ points in the plane such that:
(1) there exist 7 points in $M$ which form a convex heptagon;
(2) for any 5 points in $M$ that form a convex pentagon, there are at least two points in $M$ inside the pentagon.

Find the minimum value of $n$.

Let $M$ be a set of $n$ points in the plane such that:
(1) there exist 7 points in $M$ which form a convex heptagon;
(2) for any 5 points in $M$ that form a concave pentagon, there is a point in $M$ inside the pentagon.

Find the minimum value of $n$.

positive_text: Let $R$ be a unit-area rectangle. Place 5 points in $R$ such that no three are collinear. Determine the smallest number of triangles with area $\leq \frac{1}{4}$ that can be formed by choosing three of these points.

negatives.text: There are 5 points in a rectangle $ABCD$ with unit area such that no three are collinear. Find the minimum number of triangles with area strictly greater than $\frac{1}{4}$ and vertices chosen from these 5 points.

There are 6 points in a rectangle $ABCD$ with unit area such that no three are collinear. Find the minimum number of triangles with area no more than $\frac{1}{4}$ and vertices chosen from these 6 points.

positive_text: Let $O_1$ and $O_2$ be two intersecting circles at points $A$ and $B$. The line $DC$ passes through the center of $O_1$, intersects $O_1$ at $D$, and is tangent to $O_2$ at $C$. The line $CA$ is tangent to $O_1$ at $A$. A secant $AE$ of $O_1$ is perpendicular to $DC$. A segment $AF$ is perpendicular to $DE$ and meets it at $F$. Show that $BD$ bisects $AF$.

negatives.text: The circles $O_1$ and $O_2$ meet at points $A$ and $B$. The line $DC$ passes through $O_1$, intersects the circle $O_1$ at $D$ and is a tangent to the circle $O_2$ at $C$. Also, $CA$ is a tangent to the circle $O_2$ at $A$. The secant $AE$ of the circle $O_1$ is perpendicular to $DC$. $AF$ is perpendicular to $DE$ and meets $DE$ at $F$. Prove that $BD$ bisects the line segment $AF$.

The circles $O_1$ and $O_2$ meet at points $A$ and $B$. The line $DC$ passes through $O_1$, intersects the circle $O_1$ at $D$ and is a tangent to the circle $O_2$ at $C$. Also, $CA$ is a tangent to the circle $O_1$ at $A$. The secant $AE$ of the circle $O_1$ is parallel to $DC$. $AF$ is perpendicular to $DE$ and meets $DE$ at $F$. Prove that $BD$ bisects the line segment $AF$.

The circles $O_1$ and $O_2$ meet at points $A$ and $B$. The line $DC$ passes through $O_1$, intersects the circle $O_1$ at $D$ and is a tangent to the circle $O_2$ at $C$. Also, $CA$ is a tangent to the circle $O_1$ at $A$. The secant $AE$ of the circle $O_1$ is perpendicular to $DC$. $AF$ is perpendicular to $EC$ and meets $EC$ at $F$. Prove that $BD$ bisects the line segment $AF$.

positive_text: Let $S = \{(x, y) \mid x, y \in \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}\}$. Let $T$ be a finite set of integer points such that for each $P \in S$, there exists a point $Q \in T$ with $Q \ne P$ such that the segment $PQ$ contains no other integer points. Determine the smallest possible size of $T$.

negatives.text: Let $S = \{(a, b) \mid 1 \le a, b \le 5,\ a, b \in \mathbb{Z}\}$. Let $T$ be the set of integer points in the plane such that for any point $P$ in $S$, there exists a different point $Q$ in $T$ such that $PQ$ contains at least one integer point other than $P$ and $Q$. Find the minimum value of $|T|$.

Let $S = \{(a, b) \mid 1 \le a, b \le 5,\ a, b \in \mathbb{Z}\}$. Let $T$ be the set of integer points in the plane such that for any point $P$ in $S$, there exists a point $Q$ in $T$ such that $PQ$ contains at least two other integer points besides $P$ and $Q$. Find the minimum value of $|T|$.

positive_text: Let $O$ be the center of a circle with diameter $AB$, and let $C$ be a point on the line $AB$ extended beyond $B$. A line through $C$ intersects the circle $O$ at $D$ and $E$. The circumcircle of triangle $\triangle BOD$ has diameter $OF$. If $CF$ is extended to intersect the circumcircle of $\triangle BOD$ again at $G$, prove that $O$, $A$, $E$, and $G$ lie on a circle.

negatives.text: Let $O$ be the center of a circle with diameter $AB$, and let $C$ be a point on the line $AB$ extended beyond $B$. A line through $C$ intersects the circle at points $D$ and $E$. Let $O_1$ be the circumcircle of triangle $\triangle BOD$, and let $OF$ be a diameter of $O_1$. If $CF$ is extended to intersect $O_1$ again at $G$, prove that the points $O$, $B$, $E$, and $G$ lie on a circle.

Let $O$ be the center of a circle with diameter $AB$, and let $C$ be a point on the line $AB$ extended beyond $B$. A line through $C$ intersects the circle at points $D$ and $E$. Let $O_1$ be the circumcircle of triangle $\triangle BOD$, and let $OF$ be a diameter of $O_1$. If $CF$ is extended to intersect $O_1$ again at $G$, prove that the points $O$, $A$, $D$, and $G$ lie on a circle.

Let $O$ be the center of a circle with diameter $AB$, and let $C$ be a point on the line $AB$ extended beyond $B$. A line through $C$ intersects the circle at points $D$ and $E$. Let $O_1$ be the circumcircle of triangle $\triangle BOD$, and let $OF$ be a radius of $O_1$. If $CF$ is extended to intersect $O_1$ again at $G$, prove that the points $O$, $A$, $E$, and $G$ lie on a circle.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with angle bisector of $\angle C$ intersecting the circumcircle at $R$, the perpendicular bisector of side $BC$ at $P$, and the perpendicular bisector of side $AC$ at $Q$. Let $K$ and $L$ be the midpoints of $BC$ and $AC$, respectively. Prove that the area of triangle $\triangle RPK$ is equal to the area of triangle $\triangle RQL$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle, and let the angle bisector of $\angle BCA$ intersect the circumcircle at $R$, the perpendicular bisector of $BC$ at $P$, and the perpendicular bisector of $AB$ at $Q$. Let $K$ and $L$ be the midpoints of $BC$ and $AC$, respectively. Prove that the triangles $\triangle RPK$ and $\triangle RQL$ have the same area.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle, and let the external angle bisector of $\angle BCA$ intersect the circumcircle at $R$, the perpendicular bisector of $BC$ at $P$, and the perpendicular bisector of $AC$ at $Q$. Let $K$ and $L$ be the midpoints of $BC$ and $AC$, respectively. Prove that the triangles $\triangle RPK$ and $\triangle RQL$ have the same area.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle, and let the angle bisector of $\angle BCA$ intersect the circumcircle at $R$, the perpendicular bisector of $BC$ at $P$, and the perpendicular bisector of $AC$ at $Q$. Let $K$ and $L$ be the midpoints of $AB$ and $BC$, respectively. Prove that the triangles $\triangle RPK$ and $\triangle RQL$ have the same area.

positive_text: Let $A(-3, 0)$, $B(1, -1)$, $C(0, 3)$, and $D(-1, 3)$ be fixed points in the coordinate plane, and let $P$ be any point. Find the smallest possible value of the total distance $|PA| + |PB| + |PC| + |PD|$.

negatives.text: Given four fixed points $A(-3, 0)$, $B(1, -1)$, $C(0, 3)$, $D(-1, 3)$ and a variable point $P$ in a plane rectangular coordinate system, the minimum of $|PA|^2 + |PB|^2 + |PC|^2 + |PD|^2$ is ______.

Given four fixed points $A(-3, 0)$, $B(1, -1)$, $C(0, 3)$, $D(-1, 3)$ and a variable point $P$ in a plane rectangular coordinate system, the minimum of $|PA| + |PB| + |PC| + |PD|$ is ______, under the constraint that $P$ lies on the line $y = 1$.
Given four fixed points $A(-3, 0)$, $B(1, -1)$, $C(0, 3)$, $D(-1, 3)$ and a variable point $P$ in a plane rectangular coordinate system, the maximum of $|PA| + |PB| + |PC| + |PD|$ is ______.

positive_text: Consider a cube $ABCD-A_1B_1C_1D_1$ with edge length 1. A sphere is centered at vertex $A$ with radius $\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}$. Determine the total length of the curves formed by the intersection of the sphere and the cube.

negatives.text: Given a unit cube $ABCD-A_1B_1C_1D_1$, construct a ball with point $A$ as the center and of radius $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$. Then the length of the curves resulting from the intersection between the surfaces of the ball and cube is ______.

Given a unit cube $ABCD-A_1B_1C_1D_1$, construct a ball with point $A$ as the center and of radius $\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}$. Then the length of the curves resulting from the intersection between the surfaces of the ball and cube is ______.
Given a unit cube $ABCD-A_1B_1C_1D_1$, construct a ball with point $A$ as the center and of radius $\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}$. Then the volume of the region inside both the ball and the cube is ______.

positive_text: A sphere of radius $1$ is placed inside a regular tetrahedron with edge length $4\sqrt{6}$, moving without obstruction. Determine the area of the inner surface of the tetrahedron that remains untouched by the sphere.

negatives.text: Suppose that a ball with radius $1$ moves freely inside a regular tetrahedron with edge length $4\sqrt{6}$. Then the area of the outer surface of the container, which the ball can never touch, is ______.

Suppose that a ball with radius $1$ moves freely inside a regular tetrahedron with edge length $4\sqrt{6}$. Then the volume of the inner surface of the container, which the ball can never touch, is ______.

Suppose that a ball with radius $1$ moves freely inside a regular tetrahedron with edge length $4\sqrt{6}$. Then the area of the inner surface of the container, which the ball can always touch, is ______.

positive_text: Let $D$ be a point on segment $BC$ of triangle $ABC$ with $\angle CAD = \angle CBA$. A circle centered at $O$ passes through $B$ and $D$, and intersects $AB$ and $AD$ at points $E$ and $F$, respectively. Let $G$ be the intersection of $BF$ and $DE$, and $M$ the midpoint of $AG$. Show that $CM$ is perpendicular to $AO$.

negatives.text: Let $D$ be a point on side $BC$ of triangle $ABC$ such that $\angle CAD = \angle BCA$. A circle with center $O$ passes through $B$, $D$, and meets segments $AB$, $AD$ at $E$, $F$, respectively. Lines $BF$ and $DE$ meet at point $G$. $M$ is the midpoint of $AG$. Prove that $CM \perp AO$.

Let $D$ be a point on side $BC$ of triangle $ABC$ such that $\angle CAD = \angle CBA$. A circle with center $O$ passes through $B$, $D$, and meets segments $AB$, $AD$ at $E$, $F$, respectively. Lines $CF$ and $DE$ meet at point $G$. $M$ is the midpoint of $AG$. Prove that $CM \perp AO$.

Let $D$ be a point on side $BC$ of triangle $ABC$ such that $\angle CAD = \angle CBA$. A circle with center $O$ passes through $B$, $D$, and meets segments $AB$, $AD$ at $E$, $F$, respectively. Lines $BF$ and $DE$ meet at point $G$. $M$ is the midpoint of $AG$. Prove that $CM \parallel AO$.

positive_text: Given 12 points arranged on a circle, determine the smallest number $n$ for which there exists a set of $n$ triangles, each with vertices among the points, such that every chord connecting two of the points is a side of at least one triangle in the set.

negatives.text: Given 12 red points on a circle, find the smallest $n$ such that there exist $n$ triangles with vertices among the points, where every chord between two points is a diagonal of one of the triangles.

Given 12 red points on a circle, find the smallest $n$ such that there exist $n$ triangles with vertices among the points, where every chord between two points is a side of at least two triangles in the set.

Given 12 red points on a circle, find the smallest $n$ such that there exist $n$ triangles with vertices among the points, where every chord between two points is a side of at most one triangle in the set.

positive_text: Let $D$ lie on segment $BC$ of an acute triangle $ABC$. Consider the circle with diameter $BD$ intersecting $AB$ and $AD$ at $X$ and $P$, respectively, and the circle with diameter $CD$ intersecting $AC$ and $AD$ at $Y$ and $Q$, respectively. Drop perpendiculars from $A$ to $PX$ and $QY$, with feet at $M$ and $N$. Show that $\triangle AMN \sim \triangle ABC$ if and only if $AD$ passes through the circumcenter of $\triangle ABC$.

negatives.text: Let $D$ be a point on the side $BC$ of an acute triangle $ABC$. The circle with diameter $BD$ meets the lines $AB$ and $AD$ at $X$ and $P$. The circle with diameter $CD$ meets the lines $AC$ and $AD$ at $Y$ and $Q$. From $A$, draw lines perpendicular to $PX$ and $QY$ with feet at $M$ and $N$. Prove that $\triangle AMN \sim \triangle ABC$ if and only if the line $AD$ passes through the centroid of triangle $ABC$.

Let $D$ be a point on the side $BC$ of an acute triangle $ABC$. The circle with diameter $BD$ meets the lines $AB$ and $AD$ at $X$ and $P$. The circle with diameter $CD$ meets the lines $AC$ and $AD$ at $Y$ and $Q$. From $A$, draw lines perpendicular to $PX$ and $QY$ with feet at $M$ and $N$. Prove that $\triangle AMN \sim \triangle ABC$ if and only if the line $AD$ is perpendicular to the Euler line of triangle $ABC$.

Let $D$ be a point on the side $BC$ of an acute triangle $ABC$. The circle with diameter $BD$ meets the lines $AB$ and $AD$ at $X$ and $P$. The circle with diameter $CD$ meets the lines $AC$ and $AD$ at $Y$ and $Q$. From $A$, draw lines perpendicular to $PX$ and $QY$ with feet at $M$ and $N$. Prove that $\triangle AMN \sim \triangle ABC$ if and only if the line $AD$ bisects angle $BAC$.

positive_text: Suppose $O$ and $I$ are the circumcenter and incenter of triangle $ABC$. Show that for any point $D$ on the circumcircle of $ABC$, there exists a triangle $DEF$ such that $O$ is the circumcenter and $I$ is the incenter of triangle $DEF$.

negatives.text: Let $O$ and $I$ be the circumcenter and incenter of triangle $ABC$. Prove that for any point $D$ outside the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$, one can construct a triangle $DEF$ such that $O$ and $I$ are the circumcenter and incenter of triangle $DEF$.

Let $O$ and $I$ be the circumcenter and incenter of triangle $ABC$. Prove that for any point $D$ on the circle $O$, one can construct a triangle $DEF$ such that $O$ is the incenter and $I$ is the circumcenter of triangle $DEF$.

Let $O$ and $I$ be the circumcenter and incenter of triangle $ABC$. Prove that for any point $D$ on the circle $O$, one can construct a triangle $DEF$ such that $O$ and $I$ are the centroid and incenter of triangle $DEF$.

positive_text: Show that any arithmetic sequence of 40 positive integers must contain at least one element that cannot be expressed in the form $2^a + 3^b$, with $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$.

negatives.text: Prove that in an arithmetic progression consisting of 40 distinct positive integers, at least one of the numbers cannot be written as $2^k - 3^l$, where $k, l$ are nonnegative integers.
Prove that in an arithmetic progression consisting of 40 distinct positive integers, at least one of the numbers cannot be written as $2^k + 3^l + 1$, where $k, l$ are nonnegative integers.

positive_text: Let $O$ be the circumcenter of acute triangle $ABC$. Let $K$ be a point (not the midpoint) on side $BC$, and let $D$ be a point on the extension of $AK$ beyond $K$. If lines $BD$ and $AC$ intersect at $N$, and lines $CD$ and $AB$ intersect at $M$, show that if $OK$ is perpendicular to $MN$, then points $A$, $B$, $C$, and $D$ lie on a common circle.

negatives.text: In an acute triangle $ABC$ with circumcenter $O$, let $K$ be a point on side $BC$, and let $D$ lie on the line $AK$. Define $M$ and $N$ as the intersections of $CD$ with $AB$ and $BD$ with $AC$, respectively. Prove that if $OK$ is parallel to $MN$, then $A$, $B$, $C$, and $D$ are concyclic.

Let triangle $ABC$ be acute with circumcenter $O$. Let $K$ be a point on side $BC$, and let $D$ lie on the line $AK$. Define $M$ and $N$ as the intersections of $CD$ with $AB$ and $BD$ with $AC$, respectively. Prove that if $OK$ is perpendicular to $MN$, then $A$, $B$, and $D$ are concyclic.

In an acute triangle $ABC$ with circumcenter $O$, let $K$ be the midpoint of side $BC$, and let $D$ lie on the line $AK$. Define $M$ and $N$ as the intersections of $CD$ with $AB$ and $BD$ with $AC$, respectively. Prove that if $OK$ is perpendicular to $MN$, then $A$, $B$, $C$, and $D$ are concyclic.

positive_text: Let $P_1, P_2, \dots, P_8$ be eight distinct points arranged in a circular order. Find the minimal positive integer $n$ such that any collection of $n$ triangles with vertices chosen among these eight points necessarily contains at least two triangles sharing a side.

negatives.text: Given eight points $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_8$ on a circle, determine the smallest positive integer $n$ such that among any $n$ triangles with vertices in these eight points, there are two which share a vertex.

Given eight points $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_8$ on a circle, determine the smallest positive integer $n$ such that among any $n$ triangles with vertices in these eight points, there are two which are congruent.

Given eight points $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_8$ on a circle, determine the smallest positive integer $n$ such that among any $n$ triangles with vertices in these eight points, there are two which are disjoint (i.e., share no vertex or side).

positive_text: Let $O$ be the circumcenter of triangle $ABC$, and suppose a line through $O$ meets $AB$ and $AC$ at points $M$ and $N$, respectively. If $E$ and $F$ are the midpoints of $BN$ and $CM$, show that $\angle EOF$ is equal to $\angle BAC$.

negatives.text: Let $O$ be the circumcenter of triangle $ABC$, and suppose a line through $O$ intersects $AB$ and $AC$ at $M$ and $N$, respectively. If $E$ and $F$ are the midpoints of $BN$ and $CM$, prove that $\angle EOF = \angle B$.

Let $O$ be the circumcenter of triangle $ABC$, and suppose a line through $O$ intersects $AB$ and $AC$ at $M$ and $N$, respectively. If $E$ and $F$ are the midpoints of $BN$ and $CM$, prove that $\angle EOF = 2\angle A$.

Let $O$ be the circumcenter of triangle $ABC$, and suppose a line through $O$ intersects $AB$ and $AC$ at $M$ and $N$, respectively. If $E$ and $F$ are the midpoints of $BN$ and $CM$, prove that $\angle EOF = \angle BAC/2$.

positive_text:
Two circles $K_1$ and $K_2$ with unequal radii intersect at points $A$ and $B$. Let $C$ and $D$ be points on $K_1$ and $K_2$ such that $A$ is the midpoint of $CD$. Extending $DB$ intersects $K_1$ again at $E$, and extending $CB$ intersects $K_2$ again at $F$. Define $l_1$ and $l_2$ as the perpendicular bisectors of $CD$ and $EF$, respectively.

(1) Prove that $l_1$ and $l_2$ intersect at a unique point $P$.

(2) Show that the triangle formed by sides $CA$, $AP$, and $PE$ is a right triangle.

negatives.text:
Two circles $K_1$ and $K_2$ with different radii intersect at points $A$ and $B$. Let $C$ and $D$ be points on $K_1$ and $K_2$ such that $A$ is the midpoint of $CD$. The extension of $DB$ intersects $K_1$ at another point $E$, and the extension of $CB$ intersects $K_2$ at another point $F$. Let $l_1$ and $l_2$ be the perpendicular bisectors of $CD$ and $EF$.

(1) Show that $l_1$ and $l_2$ have a unique common point $P$.

(2) Prove that the lengths of $CA$, $AP$, and $PE$ form the sides of an isosceles triangle.

Two circles $K_1$ and $K_2$ of different radii intersect at points $A$ and $B$. Let $C$ and $D$ be points on $K_1$ and $K_2$ such that $A$ is the midpoint of $CD$. The extension of $DB$ intersects $K_1$ at another point $E$, and the extension of $CB$ intersects $K_2$ at another point $F$. Let $l_1$ and $l_2$ be the perpendicular bisectors of $CD$ and $EF$.

(1) Show that $l_1$ and $l_2$ have a unique common point $P$.

(2) Prove that the lengths of $CA$, $AP$, and $PE$ form the sides of an equilateral triangle.

Two circles $K_1$ and $K_2$ of different radii intersect at points $A$ and $B$. Let $C$ and $D$ be points on $K_1$ and $K_2$ such that $A$ is the midpoint of $CD$. The extension of $DB$ intersects $K_1$ at another point $E$, and the extension of $CB$ intersects $K_2$ at another point $F$. Let $l_1$ and $l_2$ be the perpendicular bisectors of $CD$ and $EF$.

(1) Show that $l_1$ and $l_2$ have a unique common point $P$.

(2) Prove that the lengths of $CA$, $AP$, and $PE$ form the sides of a triangle with angles in the ratio $1:2:3$.

positive_text: Let $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ be pairwise coprime positive integers with $n > 1$. Set $S = a_1 + a_2 + \dots + a_n$. For each $i$, define $d_i = \gcd(S, a_i)$ and $D_i = \gcd(\{a_j \mid j \ne i\})$. Determine the minimum value of $\prod_{i=1}^n \frac{S - a_i}{d_i D_i}$.

negatives.text: Let $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ be $n > 1$ coprime positive integers. Let $S = a_1 + a_2 + \dots + a_n$. For each $i$, define $d_i = \gcd(S, a_i)$ and $D_i = \gcd(\{a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n\} \setminus \{a_i\})$. Find the maximum of $\prod_{i=1}^n \frac{S + a_i}{d_i D_i}$.

Let $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ be $n > 1$ coprime positive integers. Let $S = a_1 + a_2 + \dots + a_n$. For each $i$, define $d_i = \gcd(S, a_i)$ and $D_i = \gcd(\{a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n\} \setminus \{a_i\})$. Find the minimum of $\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{S - a_i}{d_i D_i}$.

Let $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ be $n > 1$ coprime positive integers. Let $S = a_1 + a_2 + \dots + a_n$. For each $i$, define $d_i = \gcd(S, a_i)$ and $D_i = \gcd(\{a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n\} \setminus \{a_i\})$. Find the minimum of $\prod_{i=1}^n \frac{S - a_i}{d_i + D_i}$.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle, and let $I_B$ and $I_C$ be the centers of the B-excircle and C-excircle, respectively. Let $M_{AC}$ and $M_{AB}$ be the midpoints of sides $AC$ and $AB$, and define $B_2$ and $C_2$ as the reflections of $I_B$ and $I_C$ over $M_{AC}$ and $M_{AB}$, respectively. If the A-excircle touches side $BC$ at $D$, prove that line $AD$ is perpendicular to segment $B_2C_2$.

negatives.text: In triangle $ABC$, point $B_2$ is the reflection of the center of the B-excircle with respect to the midpoint of side $AB$, and point $C_2$ is the reflection of the center of the C-excircle with respect to the midpoint of side $AC$. The A-excircle touches side $BC$ at point $D$. Prove that $AD \perp B_2C_2$.

In triangle $ABC$, point $B_2$ is the reflection of the center of the B-excircle with respect to the midpoint of side $AC$, and point $C_2$ is the reflection of the center of the C-excircle with respect to the midpoint of side $AB$. The A-excircle touches side $BC$ at point $D$. Prove that $AD \parallel B_2C_2$.

In triangle $ABC$, point $B_2$ is the reflection of the center of the B-excircle with respect to the midpoint of side $AC$, and point $C_2$ is the reflection of the center of the C-excircle with respect to the midpoint of side $AB$. The A-excircle touches side $BC$ at point $D$. Prove that $AD$ is perpendicular to $B_2C_2$ if and only if $AB = AC$.

positive_text: Given a regular triangular pyramid $P$-$ABC$ with base edge length $1$ and height $\sqrt{2}$, find the radius of the sphere tangent to all faces of the pyramid.

negatives.text: Suppose the side of the base and the height of regular triangular pyramid $P$-$ABC$ are $1$ and $-\sqrt{2}$, respectively. Then the radius of the inscribed sphere of the pyramid is ______.
Suppose the side of the base and the height of regular triangular pyramid $P$-$ABC$ are $1$ and $\sqrt{2}$, respectively. Then the radius of the circumscribed sphere of the pyramid is ______.
Suppose the side of the base and the height of regular triangular pyramid $P$-$ABC$ are $1$ and $\sqrt{2}$, respectively. Then the volume of the inscribed sphere of the pyramid is ______.

positive_text: Let $P$ and $Q$ be convex polygons with all vertices having integer coordinates in the Euclidean plane, and let $T = P \cap Q$. Show that if $T$ is non-empty and contains no integer points, then $T$ must be a convex quadrilateral with non-zero area.

negatives.text: Let $P$ and $Q$ be convex polygons with integer-coordinate vertices in the plane, and define $T = P \cap Q$. Suppose $T$ is non-empty and contains no integer points. Prove that $T$ is a convex triangle.

Let $P$ and $Q$ be convex polygons with integer-coordinate vertices in the plane, and define $T = P \cap Q$. Suppose $T$ is non-empty and contains at least one integer point. Prove that $T$ is a convex quadrilateral.

positive_text: Let $m$ and $n$ be positive integers. Determine the least integer $N$ ($\ge m$) such that for any set of $N$ integers containing a complete set of residues modulo $m$, there exists a nonempty subset whose sum is divisible by $n$.

negatives.text: Let $m$ and $n$ be positive integers. Find the smallest integer $N$ ($\ge m$) such that if an $N$-element set of integers contains a complete residue system modulo $m$, then it has a nonempty subset whose sum is congruent to $1$ modulo $n$.

Given positive integers $m$ and $n$, find the smallest integer $N$ ($\ge m$) such that if an $N$-element set of integers contains a complete residue system modulo $m$, then it has a nonempty subset whose sum is divisible by $n$ or $n+1$.

Given positive integers $m$ and $n$, find the smallest integer $N$ ($\ge m$) such that if an $N$-element set of integers contains a complete residue system modulo $m$, then it has a nonempty subset with a sum greater than or equal to $n$.

positive_text: A regular triangular prism has all edges of length $3$. Find the volume of the sphere that passes through all the vertices of the prism.

negatives.text: Given a regular triangular prism with all edges of length $3$, find the volume of the sphere inscribed in the prism.
A regular triangular prism has all edges of length $3$. Find the volume of the sphere that passes through the midpoints of all edges.
A regular triangular prism has all edges of length $3$. Find the volume of the sphere that passes through the centroids of the triangular bases.

positive_text: Suppose $\Gamma_2$ lies entirely inside $\Gamma_1$, both being circles on the plane. Show there is a point $P$ such that for every line $\ell$ not passing through $P$, intersecting $\Gamma_1$ at $A$ and $B$, and $\Gamma_2$ at $C$ and $D$ (in the order $A, C, D, B$ along $\ell$), the equality $\angle APC = \angle DPB$ holds.

negatives.text: Let $\Gamma_2$ be a circle contained in the interior of another circle $\Gamma_1$ on the plane. Prove that there exists a point $P$ on the plane such that for any line $\ell$ that does not contain $P$, intersects $\Gamma_1$ at $A$ and $B$, and intersects $\Gamma_2$ at $C$ and $D$ in order $A, C, D, B$, then $\angle APC = \angle PBD$.

Let $\Gamma_2$ be a circle inside another circle $\Gamma_1$ on the plane. Prove that there exists a point $P$ such that for any line $\ell$ that does not contain $P$, intersects $\Gamma_1$ at $A$ and $B$, and intersects $\Gamma_2$ at $C$ and $D$ in order $A, C, D, B$, then $\angle APC = \angle DPB + 90^\circ$.

Let $\Gamma_2$ be a circle inside another circle $\Gamma_1$ on the plane. Prove that there exists a point $P$ such that for any line $\ell$ that does not contain $P$, intersects $\Gamma_1$ at $A$ and $B$, and intersects $\Gamma_2$ at $C$ and $D$ in order $A, C, D, B$, then $\angle APC = \angle DPB$ and $PA = PB$.

positive_text: Let $p$ be a prime and $A$ an infinite subset of $\mathbb{Z}$. Prove there exists a subset $B \subseteq A$ with $\left|B\right| = 2p-2$ such that the average of any $p$ distinct elements in $B$ is not in $A$.

negatives.text: Let $p$ be a prime and $A$ an infinite set of integers. Prove there exists a subset $B$ of $A$ with $\left|B\right| = 2p-2$ such that for any $p$ distinct elements in $B$, their arithmetic mean does belong to $A$.

Let $p$ be a prime and $A$ an infinite set of integers. Prove there exists a subset $B$ of $A$ with $\left|B\right| = 2p-2$ such that for any $p$ distinct elements in $B$, the geometric mean does not belong to $A$.

Let $p$ be a prime and $A$ an infinite set of integers. Prove there exists a subset $B$ of $A$ with $\left|B\right| = 2p-2$ such that for any $p-1$ distinct elements in $B$, their arithmetic mean does not belong to $A$.

positive_text:

(1) every open arc $\Gamma$ of length $\pi$ on $C$ contains at most 200 of the $z_j$;
(2) every open arc $\gamma$ of length $\frac{\pi}{3}$ on $C$ contains at most 120 of the $z_j$.
Determine the maximum value of $|z_1 + z_2 + \dots + z_{240}|$.

negatives.text:
Let $C = \{z \in \mathbb{C} \mid |z| = 1\}$ be the unit circle in the complex plane. 240 complex numbers $z_1, z_2, \dots, z_{240} \in C$ (can be repeated) satisfy the following conditions:
(1) for any open arc $\Gamma$ of length $\pi$ on $C$, there are at most 200 $j$'s $(1 \le j \le 240)$ such that $z_j \in \Gamma$;
(2) for any open arc $\gamma$ of length $\frac{\pi}{3}$ on $C$, there are at least 120 $j$'s $(1 \le j \le 240)$ such that $z_j \in \gamma$.
Find the maximum of $|z_1 + z_2 + \dots + z_{240}|$.

(1) for any open arc $\Gamma$ of length $\pi$ on $C$, there are at most 200 $j$'s $(1 \le j \le 240)$ such that $z_j \in \Gamma$;
