positive_text: Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$, and let $\Omega_{A}$ be the excircle of $\triangle ABC$ tangent to $BC$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be the points where $\omega$ and $\Omega_{A}$ intersect. Let $P$ and $Q$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $A$ to the tangents to $\Omega_{A}$ at $X$ and $Y$. Let $R$ be the intersection of the tangent to the circumcircle of $\triangle APX$ at $P$ and the tangent to the circumcircle of $\triangle AQY$ at $Q$. Show that $AR$ is perpendicular to $BC$.

negatives.text: Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$, and let $\Omega_{A}$ be the incircle of triangle $ABC$ tangent to $BC$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be the intersection points of $\omega$ and $\Omega_{A}$. Let $P$ and $Q$ be the projections of $A$ onto the tangent lines to $\Omega_{A}$ at $X$ and $Y$, respectively. The tangent line at $P$ to the circumcircle of triangle $APX$ intersects the tangent line at $Q$ to the circumcircle of triangle $AQY$ at a point $R$. Prove that $AR \perp BC$.

Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$, and let $\Omega_{A}$ be its excircle tangent to $BC$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be the intersection points of $\omega$ and $\Omega_{A}$. Let $P$ and $Q$ be the projections of $A$ onto the lines connecting $X$ and $Y$ to $A$, respectively. The tangent line at $P$ to the circumcircle of triangle $APX$ intersects the tangent line at $Q$ to the circumcircle of triangle $AQY$ at a point $R$. Prove that $AR \perp BC$.

positive_text: Suppose triangles $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$ share a common circumcircle $\omega$ and a common orthocentre $H$. If $\Omega$ is the circumcircle of the triangle formed by the lines $AA'$, $BB'$, and $CC'$, show that the points $H$, the centre of $\omega$, and the centre of $\Omega$ lie on a straight line.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$ be two triangles with the same circumcircle $\omega$ and the same centroid $G$. Let $\Omega$ be the circumcircle of the triangle determined by the lines $AA'$, $BB'$, and $CC'$. Prove that $G$, the centre of $\omega$, and the centre of $\Omega$ are collinear.

Let $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$ be two triangles with the same circumcircle $\omega$ and the same orthocentre $H$. Let $\Omega$ be the circumcircle of the triangle determined by the perpendiculars from $A$ to $A'$, $B$ to $B'$, and $C$ to $C'$. Prove that $H$, the centre of $\omega$, and the centre of $\Omega$ are collinear.

Let $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$ be two triangles with the same circumcircle $\omega$ and the same orthocentre $H$. Let $\Omega$ be the circumcircle of the triangle determined by the lines $AA'$, $BB'$, and $CC'$. Prove that $H$, the centre of $\omega$, and the point of concurrency of the altitudes of $\Omega$ are collinear.

positive_text: Let $N$ be a positive integer, and consider a square grid with $N$ rows and $N$ columns. A path moving only to the right and down is defined as a sequence where each step is either right or down. A path moving only to the right and up is defined similarly. Prove that the grid cannot be covered using fewer than $N$ such right-down or right-up paths.

negatives.text: Let $N$ be a positive integer, and consider an $N \times N$ grid. A right-up path is a sequence of grid cells where each cell is either one cell to the right or one cell above the previous cell in the sequence. Prove that the cells of the grid can be partitioned into fewer than $N$ such right-up paths.

Let $N$ be a positive integer, and consider an $N \times N$ grid. A right-down path is a sequence of grid cells where each cell is either one cell to the right or one cell down from the previous cell in the sequence. A right-up path is a sequence of grid cells where each cell is either one cell to the right or one cell up from the previous cell in the sequence. Prove that the cells of the grid cannot be partitioned into fewer than $N^2$ such paths.

Let $N$ be a positive integer, and consider an $N \times N$ grid. A right-left path is a sequence of grid cells where each cell is either one cell to the right or one cell to the left from the previous cell in the sequence. A right-up path is defined as before. Prove that the cells of the grid cannot be partitioned into fewer than $N$ such right-left or right-up paths.

positive_text:
Let triangle $ABC$ satisfy $AB < AC < BC$, with $D$ on segment $BC$ such that $D 
eq B, C$. Let $E$ lie on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ with $A$ and $E$ on opposite sides of $BC$ and $\angle BAD = \angle EAC$. Denote by $I$ the incenter of $ABC$, $I_{B}, I_{C}$ the incenters of triangles $ABD$ and $ADC$, and $J_{B}, J_{C}$ the incenters of triangles $ABE$ and $AEC$. Prove that $I_{B}, I_{C}, J_{B}, J_{C}$ lie on a circle if and only if lines $AI, I_{B}J_{C}, J_{B}I_{C}$ are concurrent.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ with $AB < AC < BC$ have a point $D$ on segment $BC$, and let $E$ be a point on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ such that $\angle BAD = \angle EAC$ and $A$ and $E$ lie on opposite sides of $BC$. Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$, and $I_{B}, I_{C}, J_{B}, J_{C}$ the incenters of triangles $ABD, ADC, ABE$, and $AEC$, respectively. Prove that $I_{B}, I_{C}, J_{B}, J_{C}$ are concyclic if and only if $AI, I_{B}J_{C}, J_{B}I_{C}$ are parallel.

Let triangle $ABC$ with $AB < AC < BC$ have a point $D$ on segment $BC$, and let $E$ be a point on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ such that $\angle BAD = \angle EAC$ and $A$ and $E$ lie on the same side of $BC$. Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$, and $I_{B}, I_{C}, J_{B}, J_{C}$ the incenters of triangles $ABD, ADC, ABE$, and $AEC$, respectively. Prove that $I_{B}, I_{C}, J_{B}, J_{C}$ are concyclic if and only if $AI, I_{B}J_{C}, J_{B}I_{C}$ concur.

Let triangle $ABC$ with $AB < AC < BC$ have a point $D$ on segment $BC$, and let $E$ be a point on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ such that $\angle BAD = \angle EAC$. Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$, and $I_{B}, I_{C}, J_{B}, J_{C}$ the incenters of triangles $ABD, ADC, ABE$, and $AEC$, respectively. Prove that $I_{B}, I_{C}, J_{B}, J_{C}$ are concyclic if and only if $AI, I_{B}J_{C}, J_{B}I_{C}$ are perpendicular.

positive_text: \text{Let } ABCD \text{ be a convex quadrilateral. Points } P \text{ and } Q \text{ lie on segments } AD \text{ and } BC \text{ respectively such that } \frac{AP}{AD} = \frac{BQ}{BC} = \frac{AB}{AB + CD}. \text{ Prove that the angle between } PQ \text{ and } AB \text{ is equal to the angle between } PQ \text{ and } CD.

negatives.text: \text{Let } ABCD \text{ be a convex quadrilateral. Suppose points } P \in AD, Q \in BC \text{ are such that } \frac{AP}{PD} = \frac{BQ}{QC} = \frac{AB}{CD} + 1. \text{ Prove that the angle between } PQ \text{ and } AB \text{ is equal to the angle between } PQ \text{ and } CD.

\text{Let } ABCD \text{ be a convex quadrilateral. Suppose points } P \in AD, Q \in BC \text{ are such that } \frac{AP}{PD} = \frac{BQ}{QC} = \left(\frac{AB}{CD}\right)^2. \text{ Prove that the angle between } PQ \text{ and } AB \text{ is equal to the angle between } PQ \text{ and } CD.

\text{Let } ABCD \text{ be a convex quadrilateral. Suppose points } P \in AD, Q \in BC \text{ are such that } \frac{AP}{PD} = \frac{BQ}{QC} = \frac{CD}{AB}. \text{ Prove that the angle between } PQ \text{ and } AB \text{ is equal to the angle between } PQ \text{ and } CD.

positive_text: Suppose a square is intersected by two mutually perpendicular lines, creating four regions. If three of these regions have an area of $1$, prove that the remaining region also has area $1$.

negatives.text: Two perpendicular lines divide a square into four parts, three of which have area $1$. Show that the fourth part has area $2$.
Two intersecting lines divide a square into four parts, three of which have area $1$. Show that the fourth part also has area $1$.
Two perpendicular lines divide a square into four parts, three of which have area $1$. Show that the fourth part has a perimeter of $1$.

positive_text: Let $M$, $N$, and $H$ be three non-collinear points. Construct a triangle such that $H$ is the orthocenter and $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of two of its sides.

negatives.text: Given three non-collinear points $M$, $N$, $H$, construct a triangle with $H$ as the centroid and $M$, $N$ as the midpoints of two sides.
Given three non-collinear points $M$, $N$, $H$, construct a triangle with $H$ as the orthocenter and $M$, $N$ as the midpoints of two of its altitudes.
Given three non-collinear points $M$, $N$, $H$, construct a triangle with $H$ as the orthocenter and $M$, $N$ as the midpoints of two of its medians.

positive_text: Determine all integers that can be expressed as the sum of the digits of a perfect square.

negatives.text: Find all possible values for the sum of the digits of a square minus one.
Find all possible values for the sum of the digits of a cube.
Find all possible values for the product of the digits of a square.

positive_text: On an $n \times n$ grid, a positive diagonal is defined as a set of cells that are parallel to the line from the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner. What is the minimum number of coins that must be placed so that each cell either contains a coin or is in the same row, column, or positive diagonal as a coin?

negatives.text: An $n \times n$ grid is given. A positive diagonal is defined as a line of cells parallel to the main diagonal. How many coins must be placed on the board such that every cell either has a coin or is in the same row, column, or negative diagonal as a coin?

An $n \times n$ grid is given. A positive diagonal is defined as a line of cells parallel to the main diagonal. How many coins must be placed on the board such that every cell either has a coin or is in the same row, column, or positive diagonal as a coin, and no two coins are on the same row, column, or diagonal?

An $n \times n$ grid is given. A positive diagonal is defined as a line of cells parallel to the main diagonal. How many coins must be placed on the board such that every cell either has a coin or is in the same row, column, or positive diagonal as a coin, and the number of coins is minimized with respect to a different cost function?

positive_text: Let $P_{1}, P_{2}, \ldots, P_{n}$ be points in the plane and $r_{1}, r_{2}, \ldots, r_{n}$ be real numbers such that for every pair $i \ne j$, the distance between $P_{i}$ and $P_{j}$ equals $r_{i} + r_{j}$. Determine the maximum possible value of $n$.

negatives.text: Let $P_{1}, P_{2}, \ldots, P_{n}$ be points in the plane and $r_{1}, r_{2}, \ldots, r_{n}$ be real numbers such that the distance between $P_{i}$ and $P_{j}$ is $r_{i} - r_{j}$ for all $i \ne j$. Determine the maximum possible value of $n$.

Suppose $P_{1}, P_{2}, \ldots, P_{n}$ are points in the plane and $r_{1}, r_{2}, \ldots, r_{n}$ are real numbers such that the distance between $P_{i}$ and $P_{j}$ is $\sqrt{r_{i} + r_{j}}$ for all $i \ne j$. Find the largest $n$ for which this is possible.

positive_text: Two circles $A$ and $B$ are given such that they are not concentric. Define a circle $D$ to bisect $A$ and $B$ if the common chord between $D$ and $A$ is a diameter of $A$, and the common chord between $D$ and $B$ is a diameter of $B$. Prove that there are infinitely many such circles $D$. Determine the set of all centers of such circles.

negatives.text: Given two circles $C$ and $C'$, define $C$ to bisect $C'$ if their common chord is a radius of $C'$. Show that for any two circles which are not concentric, there are infinitely many circles which bisect them both. Find the locus of the centers of the bisecting circles.

Given two circles $C$ and $C'$, define $C$ to bisect $C'$ if their common chord is a diameter of $C$. Show that for any two circles which are not concentric, there are infinitely many circles which bisect them both. Find the locus of the centers of the bisecting circles.

Given two circles $C$ and $C'$, define $C$ to bisect $C'$ if their common chord is a diameter of $C'$. Show that for any two circles which are not concentric, there is exactly one circle which bisects them both. Find the center of this unique bisecting circle.

positive_text: Prove that every positive integer $n > 10$ with all digits from the set $\{1,3,7,9\}$ must have a prime factor at least equal to $11$.

negatives.text: Show that any integer greater than $10$ whose digits are all members of $\{1,3,7,9\}$ has a prime factor $\leq 11$.
Show that any integer greater than $10$ whose digits are all members of $\{1,3,7,9\}$ has a prime factor $\geq 13$.
Show that any integer greater than $10$ whose digits are all members of $\{1,3,7,9\}$ has a prime factor $\geq 11$ and is also divisible by $3$.

positive_text: An infinite geometric progression $1, a, b, \ldots$ can be obtained by removing some terms from an infinite arithmetic progression starting with $1$. Determine all possible values of $a$.

negatives.text: Some terms are deleted from an infinite arithmetic progression $1, x, y, \ldots$ of real numbers to leave an infinite geometric progression $-1, a, b, \ldots$. Find all possible values of $a$.
Some terms are deleted from an infinite arithmetic progression $1, x, y, \ldots$ of real numbers to leave an infinite geometric progression $1, a, b, \ldots$. Find all possible values of $a^2$.

Some terms are deleted from an infinite arithmetic progression $1, x, y, \ldots$ of real numbers to leave an infinite geometric progression $1, a, b, \ldots$. Find all possible values of $a$ such that $a > 0$.

positive_text: Let $H$ be a convex hexagon with four diagonals of length $1$, such that all six vertices of $H$ are connected by these diagonals. Prove that for any real number $k$ satisfying $0 < k \leq 1$, there exists a unit hexagon with area $k$. Determine the maximum area achievable by such a unit hexagon.

negatives.text: A convex hexagon is called a unit if it has four diagonals of length $1$, whose endpoints include all the vertices of the hexagon. Show that there is a unit of area $k$ for any $0 < k < 1$. What is the largest possible area for a unit?

A convex hexagon is called a unit if it has four diagonals of length $1$, whose endpoints include all the vertices of the hexagon. Show that there is a unit of area $k$ for any $k \geq 1$. What is the smallest possible area for a unit?

A convex hexagon is called a unit if it has four diagonals of length $1$, whose endpoints include all the vertices of the hexagon. Show that there is a unit of area $k$ for any $0 < k \leq 1$. What is the smallest possible area for a unit?

positive_text: Let $ A $ be a subset of $ \{1,2,3, \ldots, 49\} $ such that no six elements in $ A $ form an arithmetic progression of length 6 with common difference 1. Determine the maximum size of $ A $, and count the number of subsets achieving this maximum size.

negatives.text: Let $ A $ be a subset of $ \{1,2,3, \ldots, 49\} $ such that no five consecutive integers are all in $ A $. Find the largest possible size of $ A $, and determine the number of such subsets.
Let $ A $ be a subset of $ \{1,2,3, \ldots, 49\} $ such that no six elements in $ A $ are all even. Determine the maximum size of $ A $, and count how many such subsets exist.

Let $ A $ be a subset of $ \{1,2,3, \ldots, 49\} $ such that no six elements in $ A $ are in geometric progression with common ratio 1. Find the maximum size of $ A $, and count the number of such subsets.

positive_text: Let \mathrm{ABCD} be a square. Let \mathrm{P}, \mathrm{Q} be points on sides \mathrm{BC}, \mathrm{CD} respectively, with \mathrm{BP} = \mathrm{CQ} and neither point coinciding with the vertices. Let \mathrm{X}, \mathrm{Y} be arbitrary points on lines \mathrm{AP} and \mathrm{AQ} respectively. Prove that the lengths BX, XY, and YD can form the sides of a triangle.

negatives.text: Let \mathrm{ABCD} be a square. Let \mathrm{P}, \mathrm{Q} be points on sides \mathrm{BC}, \mathrm{CD} such that BP = 2CQ. Let \mathrm{X}, \mathrm{Y} be points on lines \mathrm{AP}, \mathrm{AQ}. Show that there is a triangle with side lengths BX, XY, and YD.

Let \mathrm{ABCD} be a square. Let \mathrm{P}, \mathrm{Q} be points on sides \mathrm{BC}, \mathrm{CD} such that BP = CQ. Let \mathrm{X}, \mathrm{Y} be points on lines \mathrm{AP}, \mathrm{AQ}. Show that there is a triangle with side lengths BX^2, XY^2, and YD^2.

positive_text: Let the incircle of triangle $ABC$ touch sides $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ at points $K$, $L$, and $M$, respectively. Let $P$ be the intersection of the line through $A$ parallel to $LK$ with $MK$, and $Q$ be the intersection of the line through $A$ parallel to $MK$ with $LK$. Prove that the segment $PQ$ divides $AB$ and $AC$ in half.

negatives.text: Let the incircle of triangle $ABC$ touch sides $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ at $K$, $L$, and $M$, respectively. Let $P$ be the intersection of the line through $A$ and perpendicular to $LK$ with $MK$, and $Q$ be the intersection of the line through $A$ and perpendicular to $MK$ with $LK$. Prove that the line $PQ$ bisects the sides $AB$ and $AC$ of triangle $ABC$.

Let the incircle of triangle $ABC$ touch sides $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ at $K$, $L$, and $M$, respectively. Let $P$ be the intersection of the line through $A$ and parallel to $LK$ with $MK$, and $Q$ be the intersection of the line through $A$ and parallel to $MK$ with $LK$. Prove that the line $PQ$ bisects the side $BC$ of triangle $ABC$.

Let the incircle of triangle $ABC$ touch sides $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ at $K$, $L$, and $M$, respectively. Let $P$ be the intersection of the line through $A$ and parallel to $LK$ with $MK$, and $Q$ be the intersection of the line through $A$ and parallel to $MK$ with $LK$. Prove that the line $PQ$ trisects the sides $AB$ and $AC$ of triangle $ABC$.

positive_text:
Let $p$ be a prime number such that $p > 3$. Determine all integer pairs $(a, b)$ that satisfy the equation
$$
a^{2} + 3 a b + 2 p(a + b) + p^{2} = 0
$$

negatives.text:
Suppose $p$ is a prime greater than $3$. Find all integer pairs $(a, b)$ satisfying the equation
$$
a^{2} - 3 a b + 2 p(a + b) + p^{2} = 0
$$

Suppose $p$ is a prime greater than $3$. Find all integer pairs $(a, b)$ satisfying the equation
$$
a^{2} + 3 a b + 2 p(a + b) + 2 p^{2} = 0
$$

Suppose $p$ is a prime greater than $3$. Find all integer pairs $(a, b)$ satisfying the equation
$$
a^{2} + 3 a b + 2 p(a + b) + p^{2} < 0
$$

positive_text: Let $M$ be the midpoint of side $BC$ in triangle $ABC$. Suppose the median $AM$ intersects the incircle at two points $K$ and $L$, with $K$ closer to $A$. Given that $AK = KL = LM$, show that the side lengths of triangle $ABC$ satisfy the ratio $5 : 10 : 13$ in some order.

negatives.text: Let $M$ be the midpoint of side $BC$ of triangle $ABC$. The median $AM$ intersects the incircle at $K$ and $L$, with $K$ closer to $A$. If $AK = KL = LM$, prove that the sides of triangle $ABC$ are in the ratio $5 : 10 : 12$ in some order.

Let $M$ be the midpoint of side $BC$ in triangle $ABC$. Suppose the median $AM$ intersects the incircle at $K$ and $L$, with $K$ closer to $A$. If $AK = KL < LM$, prove that the sides of triangle $ABC$ are in the ratio $5 : 10 : 13$ in some order.

Let $M$ be the midpoint of side $BC$ in triangle $ABC$. The median $AM$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ at points $K$ and $L$, with $K$ closer to $A$. If $AK = KL = LM$, prove that the sides of triangle $ABC$ are in the ratio $5 : 10 : 13$ in some order.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ have incenter $I$, and let $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ be the images of $I$ after reflection across sides $BC, CA, AB$, respectively. If point $A$ lies on the circumcircle of triangle $A_{1}B_{1}C_{1}$, show that the points $B_{1}, C_{1}, I$, and the incenter $I_{1}$ of triangle $A_{1}B_{1}C_{1}$ are concyclic.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with incenter $I$, and $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ be the reflections of $I$ across $BC, CA, AB$. Suppose the circumcircle of triangle $A_{1}B_{1}C_{1}$ passes through $B$. Prove that $B_{1}, C_{1}, I$, and the incenter $I_{1}$ of triangle $A_{1}B_{1}C_{1}$ are concyclic.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with incenter $I$, and $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ be the reflections of $I$ across $BC, CA, AB$. Suppose the circumcircle of triangle $A_{1}B_{1}C_{1}$ passes through $A$. Prove that $B_{1}, C_{1}, I$, and the excenter $I_{1}$ of triangle $A_{1}B_{1}C_{1}$ are concyclic.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with incenter $I$, and $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ be the reflections of $I$ across $BC, CA, AB$. Suppose the circumcircle of triangle $A_{1}B_{1}C_{1}$ passes through $A$. Prove that $B_{1}, C_{1}, I$, and the centroid $G_{1}$ of triangle $A_{1}B_{1}C_{1}$ are concyclic.

positive_text: The integer lattice in the $xy$-plane is assigned one of three colours—red, blue, or green—with each colour appearing at least once. If $(0,0)$ is red and $(0,1)$ is blue, demonstrate that there are three points with distinct colours forming the vertices of a right triangle.

negatives.text: All the points with integer coordinates in the $xy$-plane are coloured using three colours, red, blue and green, each colour being used at least once. If $(0,0)$ is red and $(0,1)$ is blue, prove that there exist three points with distinct colours which form the vertices of an isosceles triangle.

All the points with integer coordinates in the $xy$-plane are coloured using three colours, red, blue and green, each colour being used at least once. If $(0,0)$ is red and $(0,1)$ is blue, prove that there exist three points with distinct colours which form the vertices of a triangle with area 1.

All the points with integer coordinates in the $xy$-plane are coloured using three colours, red, blue and green, each colour being used at least once. If $(0,0)$ is red and $(0,1)$ is blue, prove that there exist three points with distinct colours which form the vertices of a triangle with side lengths in arithmetic progression.

positive_text: Determine all positive integers $x, y$ with $x > y$ such that $(x-y)^{x+y} = x^x$.

negatives.text: Find all positive integers $a, b$ such that $(a-b)^{a-b} = a^a$.
Find all positive integers $a, b$ such that $(a-b)^{a+b} = b^b$.
Find all positive integers $a, b$ such that $(a+b)^{a-b} = a^a$.

positive_text: \text{Let } P \text{ be an interior point of a triangle } ABC. \text{ Prove that} \quad \frac{PA}{\ell_a} + \frac{PB}{\ell_b} + \frac{PC}{\ell_c} \ge \sqrt{3}, \text{ where } \ell_a, \ell_b, \ell_c \text{ are the side lengths of triangle } ABC.

negatives.text: \text{Let } P \text{ be an interior point of a triangle } ABC. \text{ Prove that} \quad \frac{PA}{a} + \frac{PB}{b} + \frac{PC}{c} > \sqrt{3}.
\text{Let } P \text{ be an interior point of a triangle } ABC. \text{ Prove that} \quad \frac{PA^2}{a^2} + \frac{PB^2}{b^2} + \frac{PC^2}{c^2} \ge \sqrt{3}.
\text{Let } P \text{ be an interior point of a triangle } ABC. \text{ Prove that} \quad \frac{PA}{b} + \frac{PB}{c} + \frac{PC}{a} \ge \sqrt{3}.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ intersecting at $E$, and let $F$ be the point where $AD$ and $BC$ meet. If $G$ and $H$ are the midpoints of $AB$ and $CD$, respectively, and $\Gamma$ is the circumcircle of triangle $EGH$, prove that $FE$ is tangent to $\Gamma$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ intersecting at $E$, and let $F$ be the intersection of $AD$ and $BC$. Let $G$ and $H$ be the midpoints of $AB$ and $CD$, respectively. If $\Gamma$ is the circumcircle of triangle $EGH$, prove that $FE$ is perpendicular to $\Gamma$.

positive_text: Let $O$ be the circumcenter of the cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$, and let $P$ be the second intersection point of the circles $ABO$ and $CDO$ (distinct from $O$), located inside triangle $DAO$. Select $Q$ on the ray $OP$ past $P$, and $R$ on the ray $OP$ past $O$. Show that $\angle QAP = \angle OBR$ is equivalent to $\angle PDQ = \angle RCO$.

negatives.text: Let $O$ be the circumcenter of cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$. Let $P$ be the second intersection of the circles $ABO$ and $CDO$, inside triangle $DAO$. Choose a point $Q$ on the extension of $OP$ beyond $P$, and a point $R$ on the extension of $OP$ beyond $O$. Prove that $\angle QAP = \angle OBR$ if and only if $\angle DPQ = \angle RCO$.

positive_text: Let $D$ be a point on side $BC$ of an acute triangle $ABC$. Let $O_{1}$ and $O_{2}$ be the circumcenters of triangles $ABD$ and $ACD$, respectively. Prove that the line connecting the circumcenter of triangle $ABC$ and the orthocenter of triangle $O_{1}O_{2}D$ is parallel to side $BC$.

negatives.text: In an acute-angled triangle $ABC$, a point $D$ lies on the segment $BC$. Let $O_{1}, O_{2}$ denote the circumcentres of triangles $ABD$ and $ACD$, respectively. Prove that the line joining the circumcentre of triangle $ABC$ and the centroid of triangle $O_{1} O_{2} D$ is parallel to $BC$.

In an acute-angled triangle $ABC$, a point $D$ lies on the segment $BC$. Let $O_{1}, O_{2}$ denote the circumcentres of triangles $ABD$ and $ACD$, respectively. Prove that the line joining the circumcentre of triangle $ABC$ and the orthocentre of triangle $O_{1} O_{2} D$ is perpendicular to $BC$.

In an acute-angled triangle $ABC$, a point $D$ lies on the segment $BC$. Let $O_{1}, O_{2}$ denote the circumcentres of triangles $ABD$ and $ACD$, respectively. Prove that the line joining the circumcentre of triangle $ABC$ and the orthocentre of triangle $O_{1} O_{2} D$ is perpendicular to the Euler line of triangle $ABC$.

positive_text: Let $\alpha, \beta$ be positive rational numbers. Suppose that there exist positive integers $p, q$ such that $\sqrt[p]{\alpha} + \sqrt[q]{\beta}$ is rational. Show that both $\sqrt[p]{\alpha}$ and $\sqrt[q]{\beta}$ must be rational.

negatives.text: Suppose $\alpha, \beta$ are positive rational numbers. Assume for some positive integers $m, n$, it is known that $\alpha^{1/n} + \beta^{1/m}$ is an irrational number. Prove that at least one of $\alpha^{1/n}$ or $\beta^{1/m}$ is irrational.

Suppose $\alpha, \beta$ are positive rational numbers. Assume for some positive integers $m, n$, it is known that $\alpha^{1/n} + \beta^{1/m}$ is a rational number. Prove that at least one of $\alpha^{1/n}$ or $\beta^{1/m}$ is a rational number.

positive_text: Given an acute triangle $ABC$ with circumcircle $\Gamma$, define $A_1$, $B_1$, and $C_1$ as the arc midpoints of $BAC$, $CBA$, and $ACB$ respectively. Prove that the inradius of triangle $A_1B_1C_1$ is at least the inradius of triangle $ABC$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with circumcircle $\Gamma$. Let $A_1$, $B_1$ and $C_1$ be respectively the midpoints of the arcs $BAC$, $CBA$ and $ACB$ of $\Gamma$. Show that the inradius of triangle $A_1B_1C_1$ is less than the inradius of triangle $ABC$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with circumcircle $\Gamma$. Let $A_1$, $B_1$ and $C_1$ be respectively the midpoints of the arcs $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ of $\Gamma$. Show that the inradius of triangle $A_1B_1C_1$ is not less than the inradius of triangle $ABC$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with circumcircle $\Gamma$. Let $A_1$, $B_1$ and $C_1$ be respectively the midpoints of the arcs $BAC$, $CBA$ and $ACB$ of $\Gamma$. Show that the inradius of triangle $A_1B_1C_1$ is greater than the inradius of triangle $ABC$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a square. When folded along the segment $EF$, vertex $A$ maps to a point $A'$ on side $BC$ (with $A' \neq C, B$) and vertex $D$ maps to $D'$. The segment $A'D'$ intersects side $CD$ at point $G$. Prove that the inradius of triangle $GCA'$ equals the sum of the inradii of triangles $GD'F$ and $A'BE$.

negatives.text: In the given figure, $ABCD$ is a square paper. It is folded along $EF$ such that $A$ goes to a point $A'$ ($A' \neq C, B$) on the side $BC$ and $D$ goes to $D'$. The line $A'D'$ cuts $CD$ in $G$. Show that the inradius of the triangle $GCA'$ is the product of the inradii of the triangles $GD'F$ and $A'BE$.

In the given figure, $ABCD$ is a square paper. It is folded along $EF$ such that $A$ goes to a point $A'$ ($A' \neq C, B$) on the side $BC$ and $D$ goes to $D'$. The line $A'D'$ cuts $CD$ in $G$. Show that the inradius of the triangle $GCA'$ is the difference of the inradii of the triangles $GD'F$ and $A'BE$.

In the given figure, $ABCD$ is a square paper. It is folded along $EF$ such that $A$ goes to a point $A'$ ($A' \neq C, B$) on the side $CD$ and $D$ goes to $D'$. The line $A'D'$ cuts $BC$ in $G$. Show that the inradius of the triangle $GCA'$ is the sum of the inradii of the triangles $GD'F$ and $A'BE$.

positive_text: Let $AB$ be a diameter of a circle $\Gamma$ and let $C$ be a point on $\Gamma$ distinct from $A$ and $B$. Let $D$ be the projection of $C$ onto $AB$. Let $K$ be a point on $CD$ such that the semiperimeter of triangle $ADK$ is equal to the length of $AC$. Prove that the $A$-excircle of triangle $ADK$ touches $\Gamma$.

negatives.text: Let $AB$ be a diameter of a circle $\Gamma$ and $C$ be a point on $\Gamma$ different from $A$ and $B$. Let $D$ be the foot of perpendicular from $C$ onto $AB$. Let $K$ be a point on segment $CD$ such that $AC$ is equal to the perimeter of triangle $ADK$. Prove that the excircle of triangle $ADK$ opposite $A$ is tangent to $\Gamma$.

Let $AB$ be a diameter of a circle $\Gamma$ and $C$ be a point on $\Gamma$ different from $A$ and $B$. Let $D$ be the foot of perpendicular from $C$ onto $AB$. Let $K$ be a point on segment $CD$ such that $AC$ is equal to the semiperimeter of triangle $ADK$. Prove that the incircle of triangle $ADK$ is tangent to $\Gamma$.

Let $AB$ be a diameter of a circle $\Gamma$ and $C$ be a point on $\Gamma$ different from $A$ and $B$. Let $D$ be the foot of perpendicular from $C$ onto $AB$. Let $K$ be a point on segment $CD$ such that $AC$ is equal to the semiperimeter of triangle $ADK$. Prove that the excircle of triangle $ADK$ opposite $K$ is tangent to $\Gamma$.

positive_text: Let $\Gamma_{1}$ and $\Gamma_{2}$ be circles with distinct radii, centred at $O_{1}$ and $O_{2}$, intersecting at $A$ and $B$. Suppose $O_{1}$ lies outside $\Gamma_{2}$ and $O_{2}$ lies outside $\Gamma_{1}$. The tangent to $\Gamma_{1}$ at $B$ intersects $\Gamma_{2}$ at a second point $C$, and the tangent to $\Gamma_{2}$ at $B$ intersects $\Gamma_{1}$ at a second point $D$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be the second intersections of the angle bisectors of $\angle D A B$ and $\angle C A B$ with $\Gamma_{1}$ and $\Gamma_{2}$, respectively. Let $P$ and $Q$ be the circumcentres of triangles $A C D$ and $X A Y$. Prove that the line $P Q$ is the perpendicular bisector of $O_{1} O_{2}$.

negatives.text: Let $\Gamma_{1}$ and $\Gamma_{2}$ be circles of different radii, with centres $O_{1}$ and $O_{2}$, intersecting at $A$ and $B$. The tangent to $\Gamma_{1}$ at $B$ intersects $\Gamma_{2}$ again at $C$, and the tangent to $\Gamma_{2}$ at $B$ intersects $\Gamma_{1}$ again at $D$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be the second intersections of the bisectors of $\angle D A B$ and $\angle C A B$ with $\Gamma_{1}$ and $\Gamma_{2}$, respectively. Let $P$ and $Q$ be the incentres of triangles $A C D$ and $X A Y$. Prove that $P Q$ is the perpendicular bisector of $O_{1} O_{2}$.

Let $\Gamma_{1}$ and $\Gamma_{2}$ be circles of different radii, with centres $O_{1}$ and $O_{2}$, intersecting at $A$ and $B$. The tangent to $\Gamma_{1}$ at $B$ intersects $\Gamma_{2}$ again at $C$, and the tangent to $\Gamma_{2}$ at $B$ intersects $\Gamma_{1}$ again at $D$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be the second intersections of the bisectors of $\angle D A B$ and $\angle C A B$ with $\Gamma_{1}$ and $\Gamma_{2}$, respectively. Let $P$ and $Q$ be the circumcentres of triangles $A C D$ and $X A Y$. Prove that $P Q$ is the perpendicular bisector of $O_{1} B$.

positive_text: A stromino is a $3 \times 1$ rectangle. Prove that it is impossible to tile a $5 \times 5$ board, divided into unit squares, using 16 strominoes, where each stromino covers three adjacent unit squares and each unit square is overlapped by one or two strominoes.

negatives.text: A stromino is a $3 \times 1$ rectangle. Show that a $5 \times 5$ board divided into twenty-five $1 \times 1$ squares cannot be covered by 16 strominoes such that each stromino covers exactly three unit squares and every unit square is covered by either one or three strominoes.

A stromino is a $3 \times 1$ rectangle. Show that a $6 \times 6$ board divided into thirty-six $1 \times 1$ squares cannot be covered by 16 strominoes such that each stromino covers exactly three unit squares and every unit square is covered by either one or two strominoes.

A stromino is a $3 \times 1$ rectangle. Show that a $5 \times 5$ board divided into twenty-five $1 \times 1$ squares cannot be covered by 16 strominoes such that each stromino covers exactly four unit squares and every unit square is covered by either one or two strominoes.

positive_text: Betal places $2021$ points on the plane such that no three are collinear, and constructs all the line segments connecting them. He randomly selects $1011$ of these segments and labels their midpoints. Then, he selects a segment whose midpoint has not been labeled and asks Vikram to use only a straightedge to construct the missing midpoint. Is it always possible for Vikram to fulfill the request?

negatives.text: Betal marks $2021$ points on the plane such that no three are collinear, and draws all possible line segments joining these. He then chooses any $1010$ of these line segments, and marks their midpoints. Finally, he chooses a line segment whose midpoint is not marked yet, and challenges Vikram to construct its midpoint using only a straightedge. Can Vikram always complete this challenge?

Betal marks $2021$ points on the plane such that no three are collinear, and draws all possible line segments joining these. He then chooses any $1011$ of these line segments, and marks their endpoints instead of their midpoints. Finally, he chooses a line segment whose midpoint is not marked yet, and challenges Vikram to construct its midpoint using only a straightedge. Can Vikram always complete this challenge?

Betal marks $2021$ points on the plane such that no three are collinear, and draws all possible line segments joining these. He then chooses any $1011$ of these line segments, and marks their midpoints. Finally, he chooses a line segment whose midpoint is not marked yet, and challenges Vikram to construct its midpoint using only a compass. Can Vikram always complete this challenge?

positive_text: Let $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be strictly increasing and let $k$ be a positive integer. Assume there exist primes $q_1, q_2, \ldots, q_k$ and integers $t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_k$ such that for all $1 \le i \le k$, the set $\{f(q_i r + t_i) \mid r = 1, 2, \ldots\}$ is an infinite arithmetic progression. Prove there exists an integer $b$ such that $f(b + 1), f(b + 2), \ldots, f(b + k)$ is an arithmetic progression.

negatives.text: Let $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be increasing and $n$ a natural number. Suppose there exist primes $p_1, \ldots, p_n$ and natural numbers $s_1, \ldots, s_n$ such that the set $\{f(p_i r + s_i) \mid r = 1, 2, \ldots\}$ is an infinite geometric progression for each $i$. Prove that $f(a + 1), \ldots, f(a + n)$ is a geometric progression for some natural number $a$.

Let $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be increasing and $n$ a natural number. Suppose there exist primes $p_1, \ldots, p_n$ and natural numbers $s_1, \ldots, s_n$ such that the set $\{f(p_i r + s_i) \mid r = 1, 2, \ldots\}$ is a finite arithmetic progression for each $i$. Prove there exists a natural number $a$ such that $f(a + 1), \ldots, f(a + n)$ is an arithmetic progression.

Let $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be increasing and $n$ a natural number. Suppose there exist primes $p_1, \ldots, p_n$ and natural numbers $s_1, \ldots, s_n$ such that the set $\{f(p_i r + s_i) \mid r = 1, 2, \ldots\}$ is an arithmetic progression for each $i$, but $f$ is not necessarily strictly increasing. Prove that there exists a natural number $a$ such that $f(a + 1), \ldots, f(a + n)$ is an arithmetic progression.

positive_text: Let a sphere be placed on a flat surface with a distinct point labeled on its surface. Show that it is possible to roll the sphere along a closed polygonal path on the plane such that the labeled point ends up at the top of the sphere when it returns to its original position. The rolling must be such that the sphere actually moves along the path and does not spin in place.

negatives.text: A spherical ball is placed on a flat plane with a marked point. Show that it is possible to roll the ball along a closed polygon on the plane such that the marked point ends up at the bottom of the ball when it returns to its initial position. The ball must not roll in place.

A spherical ball is placed on a flat plane with a marked point. Show that it is possible to roll the ball along a closed polygon on the plane such that the marked point ends up at the top of the ball when it returns to its initial position. The ball must be allowed to roll in place.

A spherical ball is placed on a flat plane with a marked point. Show that it is possible to roll the ball along a non-closed polygon on the plane such that the marked point ends up at the top of the ball when it returns to its initial position. The ball must not roll in place.

positive_text: Eleven individuals are seated in a circle at equal intervals. They each hold some of the cards numbered from $1$ to $11$. At the start, each person holds exactly one card, and the cards are distributed in counter-clockwise order. In one move, a person may pass a card $i$ to an adjacent neighbor if the positions of the cards $i-1$, $i$, and $i+1$ (with card $0$ identified as card $11$ and card $12$ as card $1$) do **not** form the vertices of an acute triangle before and after the transfer. Prove that no individual can ever end up holding all $11$ cards.

negatives.text: There are $11$ men sitting around a circular table with equal distances and $11$ cards with numbers $1,2,\ldots,11$ on them are dealt among them. It is possible that one has no cards and the other has more than one. In each step one can give one of his cards to his adjacent individual if the card number $i$ has the following property: before and after this stage, the places of the cards with numbers $i-1$, $i$ and $i+1$ are **not** the vertices of a right-angled triangle. (card $0$ is the same as card $11$, and card $12$ is the same as card $1$) At the beginning the cards $1$ to $11$ are dealt among them counter-clockwise. (everyone has exactly one card) Prove that there will never be a man who has all the cards.

There are $11$ men sitting around a circular table with equal distances and $11$ cards with numbers $1,2,\ldots,11$ on them are dealt among them. It is possible that one has no cards and the other has more than one. In each step one can give one of his cards to his adjacent individual if the card number $i$ has the following property: before and after this stage, the places of the cards with numbers $i-1$, $i$ and $i+1$ are **not** the vertices of an **obtuse**-angled triangle. (card $0$ is the same as card $11$, and card $12$ is the same as card $1$) At the beginning the cards $1$ to $11$ are dealt among them counter-clockwise. (everyone has exactly one card) Prove that there will never be a man who has all the cards.

There are $11$ men sitting around a circular table with equal distances and $11$ cards with numbers $1,2,\ldots,11$ on them are dealt among them. It is possible that one has no cards and the other has more than one. In each step one can give one of his cards to his adjacent individual if the card number $i$ has the following property: before and after this stage, the places of the cards with numbers $i-1$, $i$ and $i+1$ **do** form the vertices of an acute-angled triangle. (card $0$ is the same as card $11$, and card $12$ is the same as card $1$) At the beginning the cards $1$ to $11$ are dealt among them counter-clockwise. (everyone has exactly one card) Prove that there will never be a man who has all the cards.

positive_text:
Let $p$ be an odd prime number. Define a polynomial

$$
f(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{n} a_{j}x^{j}
$$
to be $i$-residue if the sum of its coefficients with degree strictly greater than $p-1$ is congruent to $i$ modulo $p$. Prove that the set $\{f(1), f(2), \dots, f(p-1)\}$ is a complete residue system modulo $p$ if and only if $f(x), f(x)^2, \dots, f(x)^{p-2}$ are 0-residue and $f(x)^{p-1}$ is 1-residue.

negatives.text:
Let $p$ be an odd prime number. We say a polynomial

$$
f(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{n} a_{j}x^{j} \text{ is } i\text{-residue if } \sum_{p-1 < j, j > 0} a_{j} \equiv i \pmod{p}.
$$

Show that $\{f(1), \dots, f(p-1)\}$ is a complete residue system modulo $p$ if and only if polynomials $f(x), \dots, f(x)^{p-2}$ are 1-residue and $(f(x))^{p-1}$ is 0-residue.

Let $p$ be an odd prime number. Define a polynomial

$$
f(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{n} a_{j}x^{j} \text{ to be } i\text{-residue if } \sum_{j > p-1} a_{j}^{2} \equiv i \pmod{p}.
$$

Show that $\{f(1), \dots, f(p-1)\}$ is a complete residue system modulo $p$ if and only if polynomials $f(x), \dots, f(x)^{p-2}$ are 0-residue and $(f(x))^{p-1}$ is 1-residue.

positive_text: Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of an acute triangle $ABC$. Let $D$ be the midpoint of arc $\widearc{BAC}$ not containing $B$ and $C$, and let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$. The line $DI$ intersects $BC$ at $E$ and intersects $\omega$ again at $F$. If a line through $E$ parallel to $AI$ intersects $AF$ at $P$, prove that $PE$ bisects $\angle BPC$.

negatives.text: Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of an acute triangle $ABC$. Let $D$ be the midpoint of arc $\widearc{BC}$ not containing $A$, and let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$. The line $DI$ intersects $BC$ at $E$ and $\omega$ again at $F$. If a line through $E$ parallel to $AI$ intersects $AF$ at $P$, prove that $PE$ bisects $\angle BPC$.

Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of an acute triangle $ABC$. Let $D$ be the midpoint of arc $\widearc{BAC}$, and let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$. The line $DI$ intersects $BC$ at $E$ and $\omega$ again at $F$. If a line through $E$ perpendicular to $AI$ intersects $AF$ at $P$, prove that $PE$ bisects $\angle BPC$.

positive_text: Let four rigid segments be connected at their endpoints in space to form a flexible quadrilateral. If the quadrilateral is non-planar, select one point on each segment such that these four points are coplanar. Show that such a selection is always possible, regardless of the configuration of the quadrilateral.

negatives.text: Four metal pieces are joined to each other to form a quadrilateral in the space. The angle between them can vary freely. In a case that the quadrilateral is not planar, we mark one point of each piece such that the points lie on a sphere. Prove that these four points are always co-spherical as the quadrilateral varies.

Four metal pieces are joined to each other to form a quadrilateral in the space. The angle between them can vary freely. In a case that the quadrilateral is not planar, we mark one point of each piece such that the points lie in a plane. Prove that these four points are always colinear as the quadrilateral varies.

Four metal pieces are joined to each other to form a quadrilateral in the space. The angle between them can vary freely. In a case that the quadrilateral is not planar, we mark one point of each piece such that the points lie in a plane. Prove that these four points are always equidistant from a fixed point as the quadrilateral varies.

positive_text: Consider an escalator at ``Champion Butcher'' metro station whose speed depends on the number of people on it. Specifically, if $m$ persons are on it, the escalator moves with speed $\frac{1}{m^{\alpha}}$, where $\alpha$ is a positive constant. Suppose $n$ individuals wish to travel up the escalator. If the escalator's total length is $l$, what is the minimal time required for all $n$ persons to reach the top? (Assume the persons can use the escalator simultaneously at any time).

negatives.text: At ``Champion Butcher'' metro station, the speed of the escalator depends on the number of individuals on it. If $m$ persons are on the escalator, its speed is $m^{\alpha}$, where $\alpha$ is a positive constant. If $n$ people want to ascend the escalator of length $l$, what is the minimum time required for all $n$ people to reach the top? (Assume all $n$ people can use the escalator at the same time).

At ``Champion Butcher'' metro station, the speed of the escalator depends on the square of the number of individuals on it. If $m$ persons are on the escalator, its speed is $m^{-\alpha^2}$, where $\alpha$ is a positive constant. If $n$ people want to ascend the escalator of length $l$, what is the minimum time required for all $n$ people to reach the top? (Assume all $n$ people can use the escalator at the same time).

At ``Champion Butcher'' metro station, the speed of the escalator is $m^{-\alpha}$ when $m$ persons are on it, where $\alpha$ is a positive constant. If $n$ people want to ascend the escalator of length $l$, what is the maximum time required for all $n$ people to reach the top? (Assume all $n$ people can use the escalator at the same time).

positive_text: Determine the minimal positive integer $ n $ for which there are $ n $ real values $ x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n $ with $ x_i \in (-1,1) $ for all $ i $, and such that $ \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i = 0 $ and $ \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i^2 = 20 $.

negatives.text: Find the smallest positive integer $ n $ such that there exist $ n $ real numbers in the interval $ [-1,1] $ such that their sum is zero and the sum of their squares equals $ 20 $.
Find the smallest positive integer $ n $ such that there exist $ n $ real numbers in the interval $ (-1,1) $ such that their sum is zero and the sum of their cubes equals $ 20 $.
Find the smallest positive integer $ n $ such that there exist $ n $ real numbers in the interval $ (-1,1) $ such that their product is zero and the sum of their squares equals $ 20 $.

positive_text: Let $m$ and $n$ be nonnegative integers. On an infinite hexagonal grid, a piece called the Phoenix moves by first moving $m$ cells in any of the six cardinal directions, and then turning 60 degrees clockwise and moving $n$ cells. Determine the maximum number of distinct cells such that it is impossible to move from one to another using a finite number of Phoenix moves.

negatives.text: Let $m$ and $n$ be nonnegative integers. On a regular hexagonal grid, a Phoenix piece moves by first moving $m$ cells in one of the six directions, and then turning 60 degrees counterclockwise and moving $n$ cells in the new direction. Determine the maximum number of cells such that one cannot reach another with a finite number of Phoenix moves.

Let $m$ and $n$ be nonnegative integers. On a regular hexagonal grid, a Phoenix piece moves by first moving $m^2$ cells in one of the six directions, and then turning 60 degrees clockwise and moving $n$ cells in the new direction. Determine the maximum number of cells such that one cannot reach another with a finite number of Phoenix moves.

Let $m$ and $n$ be nonnegative integers. On a regular hexagonal grid, a Phoenix piece moves by first moving $m$ cells in one of the six directions, and then turning 120 degrees clockwise and moving $n$ cells in the new direction. Determine the maximum number of cells such that one cannot reach another with a finite number of Phoenix moves.

positive_text: Let four distinct points $A$, $B$, $C$, and $D$ lie in this order on a straight line $\ell$. Define arcs $\Gamma_1$ and $\Gamma_2$ with endpoints $\{A, B\}$ and arcs $\Gamma'_1$ and $\Gamma'_2$ with endpoints $\{C, D\}$ on the same side of $\ell$. Suppose $\Gamma_1$ is tangent to $\Gamma'_1$ and $\Gamma_2$ is tangent to $\Gamma'_2$. Prove that the external common tangent to $\Gamma_1$ and $\Gamma'_2$ and the external common tangent to $\Gamma'_1$ and $\Gamma_2$ intersect on $\ell$.

negatives.text: Let $X$, $Y$, $X'$, and $Y'$ lie on a line $l$ in that order. Consider arcs $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ with endpoints $\{X, Y\}$ and arcs $\omega'_1$ and $\omega'_2$ with endpoints $\{X', Y'\}$ on the same side of $l$. Suppose $\omega_1$ is tangent to $\omega'_2$ and $\omega_2$ is tangent to $\omega'_1$. Prove that the external common tangent of $\omega_1$ and $\omega'_2$ and the external common tangent of $\omega'_1$ and $\omega_2$ meet on $l$.

Let $X$, $Y$, $X'$, and $Y'$ be points on a line $l$ in that order. Consider arcs $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ with endpoints $\{X, Y\}$ and arcs $\omega'_1$ and $\omega'_2$ with endpoints $\{X', Y'\}$ on the same side of $l$. Suppose $\omega_1$ is tangent to $\omega'_1$ and $\omega_2$ is tangent to $\omega'_2$. Prove that the internal common tangent of $\omega_1$ and $\omega'_2$ and the internal common tangent of $\omega'_1$ and $\omega_2$ meet on $l$.

Let $X$, $Y$, $X'$, and $Y'$ lie on a line $l$ in that order. Consider arcs $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ with endpoints $\{X, Y\}$ and arcs $\omega'_1$ and $\omega'_2$ with endpoints $\{X', Y'\}$ on the same side of $l$. Suppose $\omega_1$ is tangent to $\omega'_1$ and $\omega_2$ is tangent to $\omega'_2$. Prove that the external common tangent of $\omega_1$ and $\omega'_2$ and the internal common tangent of $\omega'_1$ and $\omega_2$ meet on $l$.

positive_text: Determine the largest size of a set of permutations of $\{1, 2, \ldots, 2014\}$ with the property that for any distinct $a, b$, there is at most one permutation where $b$ occurs after $a$.

negatives.text: Find the maximum number of permutations of the set $\{1, 2, \ldots, 2014\}$ such that for each two distinct numbers $a$ and $b$ of this set, one could find at most one permutation in which $b$ has appeared exactly after $a$ or before $a$.

Find the maximum number of permutations of the set $\{1, 2, \ldots, 2014\}$ such that for each two distinct numbers $a$ and $b$ of this set, one could find at least one permutation in which $b$ has appeared exactly after $a$.

positive_text: Let $A$ be a simple polygon with perimeter $p$. A polygon $A$ is called **rotund** if for every pair of points $x, y$ on the perimeter of $A$ with Euclidean distance $\leq 1$, the shorter arc between $x$ and $y$ along the perimeter of $A$ is at most $\frac{p}{4}$. Prove that a disk of radius $\frac{1}{4}$ can be inscribed entirely within $A$.

negatives.text: Let $A$ be a polygon with perimeter $p$. Suppose that for any two points $x$ and $y$ on the perimeter with Euclidean distance at most $1$, the shorter boundary arc between them is at least $\frac{p}{4}$. Prove that a circle of radius $\frac{1}{4}$ can be inscribed in $A$.

positive_text: Suppose a tree with $n$ vertices is labeled with distinct numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$. In each step, one may pick an unused edge and swap the labels at its endpoints. After all edges have been used, prove that the resulting permutation of labels is a single $n$-cycle.

negatives.text: The vertices of an $n$-vertex tree are labeled $1, 2, \ldots, n$. At each stage one can choose an edge that has not been selected before, and swap the labels of its two ends, until all of the edges have been selected. Show that the final permutation of the labels is the identity permutation.

The vertices of an $n$-vertex tree are labeled $1, 2, \ldots, n$. At each stage one can choose an edge that has not been selected before, and swap the labels of its two ends, until all of the edges have been selected. Show that the final permutation of the labels is a product of disjoint cycles of length $\leq n/2$.

positive_text: Let $D$ be a variable point on side $BC$ of triangle $ABC$. Let $I$, $I_1$, and $I_2$ be the incenters of triangles $ABC$, $ABD$, and $ACD$, respectively. Define $M$ and $N$ as the second points of intersection (other than $I$) of the circumcircles of triangles $IAI_1$ and $IAI_2$ with the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$. Show that the line $MN$ always passes through a fixed point in the plane as $D$ moves along $BC$.

negatives.text: Let $D$ be a variable point on side $BC$ of triangle $ABC$. The incenters of triangles $ABC$, $ABD$ and $ACD$ are $I$, $I_1$ and $I_2$, respectively. Points $M$ and $N$ are the second intersection points of circumcircles of triangles $IBI_1$ and $IBI_2$ with the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$, respectively. Prove that as $D$ varies on side $BC$, line $MN$ passes through a fixed point in the plane.

Let $D$ be a variable point on side $BC$ of triangle $ABC$. The incenters of triangles $ABC$, $ABD$ and $ACD$ are $I$, $I_1$ and $I_2$, respectively. Points $M$ and $N$ are the second intersection points of circumcircles of triangles $IAI_1$ and $IAI_2$ with the incircle of triangle $ABC$, respectively. Prove that as $D$ varies on side $BC$, line $MN$ passes through a fixed point in the plane.

Let $D$ be a variable point on side $BC$ of triangle $ABC$. The incenters of triangles $ABC$, $ABD$ and $ACD$ are $I$, $I_1$ and $I_2$, respectively. Points $M$ and $N$ are the second intersection points of circumcircles of triangles $IAI_1$ and $IAI_2$ with the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$, respectively. Prove that as $D$ varies on side $BC$, the midpoint of $MN$ lies on a fixed circle in the plane.

positive_text: Let $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ and $b_1, b_2, \dots, b_n$ be $2n$ positive numbers. Suppose that all the $a_i$'s are distinct and can be partitioned into two subsets with equal total sum, and the same is true for the $b_i$'s. Prove that there exists a non-intersecting polygon with $2n$ sides aligned with the coordinate axes, where the horizontal sides are given by the $a_i$'s and the vertical sides by the $b_i$'s.

negatives.text: Let $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ and $b_1, b_2, \dots, b_n$ be $2n$ positive numbers. Suppose all the $a_i$'s and $b_i$'s are equal and can be partitioned into two subsets with equal sum. Prove that there exists a simple $2n$-gon with sides parallel to the coordinate axes such that the horizontal edges are the $a_i$'s and the vertical edges are the $b_i$'s.

positive_text: Let there be a flat terrain with a canyon represented as an infinite strip of width $\omega$. On one side lies a polyhedron with diameter $d$, and on the other, a cavity with radius $d$. The objective is to roll the polyhedron across the canyon so that it can be dropped into the cavity, maintaining at least one point of contact with the ground at all times. A bridge of width $\frac{d}{10}$ has been constructed over the canyon. Prove that this is feasible.

negatives.text: Consider a perfectly straight land having a canyon in the form of an infinite strip of width $\omega$. A polyhedron of diameter $d$ is placed on one side of the canyon and a cavity of radius $d$ on the other. A bridge of width $\frac{d}{10}$ is built over the canyon. The polyhedron must be moved across the canyon to the cavity, maintaining at least two contact points with the ground at all times. Prove that it is possible to drop the polyhedron into the cavity.

Consider a perfectly straight land having a canyon in the form of an infinite strip of width $\omega$. The polyhedron must be dropped into the cavity from a height of $\frac{d}{2}$, while maintaining at least one contact point with the ground at all times. Prove that it is possible to drop the polyhedron into the cavity.

The polyhedron must be dropped into the cavity such that at all times during its motion, the center of mass remains above the bridge. Prove that it is possible to drop the polyhedron into the cavity.

positive_text:
A non-empty collection $ T $ of positive real numbers is defined to be **powerful** if, for any two different elements $ x $ and $ y $, at least one of $ x^y $ or $ y^x $ also belongs to $ T $.

a) Give an example of a powerful set with four elements.
b) Show that a finite powerful set can contain no more than four elements.

negatives.text:
A non-empty set $ S $ of positive real numbers is called **powerful** if for any two distinct elements $ a $ and $ b $, both of the numbers $ a^b $ and $ b^a $ are elements of $ S $.

a) Present an example of a powerful set having four elements.
b) Prove that a finite powerful set cannot have more than four elements.

A non-empty set $ S $ of positive real numbers is called **powerful** if for any two distinct elements $ a $ and $ b $, at least one of the numbers $ a^b $ or $ b^a $ is not in $ S $.

a) Present an example of a powerful set having four elements.
b) Prove that a finite powerful set cannot have more than four elements.

A non-empty set $ S $ of positive real numbers is called **powerful** if for any two distinct elements $ a $ and $ b $, at least one of the numbers $ a^b $ or $ b^a $ is an element of $ S $, and $ a $ and $ b $ are both greater than 1.

a) Present an example of a powerful set having four elements.
b) Prove that a finite powerful set cannot have more than four elements.

positive_text:
Let us define a **Lattice-aligned polygon** as a polygon in three-dimensional space where each edge is aligned with one of the coordinate axes.

a) In any such polygon, consecutive edges meet at right angles lying in the $xy$, $yz$, or $zx$ planes. Show that the counts of angles in these planes are congruent modulo 2.
b) A **Centrally Symmetric Lattice-aligned polygon** is one for which there exists a point equidistant from all vertices. Prove that if a six-sided Lattice-aligned polygon is non-planar, it is centrally symmetric.
c) Does there exist a Lattice-aligned polygon with 2014 distinct vertices such that a plane intersects each edge in a point that is not a vertex?
d) For natural numbers *a*, *b*, and *c$ with $a, b, c > 1$, prove that one can construct three points in a plane with mutual distances *a*, *b*, and *c$ if and only if there exists a Lattice-aligned polygon with *a*, *b*, and *c$ edges along each of the three coordinate axes.

negatives.text:

a) For such a polygon, adjacent edges form right angles in one of the coordinate planes. Prove that the number of such angles in the $xy$, $yz$, and $zx$ planes are all congruent modulo 2.
b) A Latticelike polygon is called an Inscribed Latticelike polygon if there exists a point in space that has equal distances from every vertex of the polygon. Prove that if a hexagon is not planar (i.e. there doesn't exist a plane containing all six vertices), then it is a centrally symmetric polygon.
c) Does there exist a Latticelike 2014-gon with distinct vertices for which there exists a plane that intersects every edge of it at its endpoints?
d) *a*, *b* and *c* are three natural numbers greater than 1. Prove that one can find three points in plane having mutual distance equal to *a*, *b$ and *c$ if and only if there exists a Latticelike polygon with *a*, *b*, and *c$ edges in each of the two coordinate directions.

b) A Latticelike polygon is called an Inscribed Latticelike polygon if there exists a point in space that has equal distances from every vertex of the polygon. Prove that if a hexagon is not planar (i.e. there doesn't exist a plane containing all six vertices), then it is an Inscribed Latticelike polygon.
c) Does there exist a Latticelike 2015-gon with distinct vertices for which there exists a plane that intersects every edge of it in an inner point?

positive_text: Determine the largest number of $1 \times 2$ rectangles aligned with the coordinate axes such that the intersection of any two rectangles has an area of $1$.

positive_text: Each of 27 cards has a number (1, 2, or 3), a type (circle, square, or triangle), and a color (white, grey, or black). A **match** consists of three cards such that for each attribute (number, type, color), the values are either all the same or all different. For example, a triple with distinct numbers, distinct types, and the same color is a **match**. What is the maximum number of cards that can be selected so that no **match** is formed?

If a line perpendicular to $EF$ at $M$ and another perpendicular to $BC$ at $N$ meet at point $P$, show that $P$ lies on the median from $A$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle A \ne 90^\circ$. Points $E, F$ are the feet of the altitudes from $B, C$ to $AC, AB$, respectively. positive_text: Let $m$ and $n$ be positive integers. A group of $mn$ individuals are arranged in a grid of size $m \times n$. Among them, some are police officers, and the rest are guests. A subset of the guests may be criminals. The task is to determine whether any criminal is present among the guests. A police officer can observe all their adjacent individuals and can determine whether each is a criminal or not. However, each criminal will select one of their adjacent individuals (likely an officer) to threaten, and any threatened officer will falsely deny the presence of a criminal among their neighbors. Determine the minimal number of officers required so that the group can be positioned in the grid to always detect the presence of a criminal (or confirm none exist).

negatives.text: Let $m$ and $n$ be positive integers. A group of $mn$ individuals are arranged in a grid of size $m \times n$. Some are police officers, and the rest are guests. Any criminal among the guests will threaten one of their adjacent people (likely an officer), but a threatened officer will falsely confirm the presence of a criminal among their neighbors. Determine the minimum number of officers required such that the grid can be arranged to always detect the presence of a criminal.

Let $m$ and $n$ be positive integers. A grid of $m \times n$ people includes police officers and guests, some of whom may be criminals. A criminal threatens one of their adjacent individuals, and the threatened person is always an officer. A threatened officer will refuse to speak entirely. Determine the minimum number of officers required to always detect the presence of a criminal.

Let $m$ and $n$ be positive integers. A grid of $m \times n$ people includes police officers and guests. A criminal threatens two adjacent individuals (not one) and each threatened officer will deny the presence of a criminal among their neighbors. Determine the minimum number of officers required such that the presence of a criminal is always detectable.

positive_text:
Let $p$ be an odd prime number. Find all $\frac{p-1}{2}$-tuples $(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{\frac{p-1}{2}}) \in \mathbb{Z}_{p^2}^{\frac{p-1}{2}}$ such that
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{\frac{p-1}{2}} x_i \equiv \sum_{i=1}^{\frac{p-1}{2}} x_i^2 \equiv \dots \equiv \sum_{i=1}^{\frac{p-1}{2}} x_i^{\frac{p-1}{2}} \equiv 0 \pmod{p}.
$$

negatives.text:
Let $p$ be an odd prime number. Find all $\frac{p-1}{2}$-tuples $(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{\frac{p-1}{2}}) \in \mathbb{Z}_{p^2}^{\frac{p-1}{2}}$ such that
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{\frac{p-1}{2}} x_i^k \equiv 1 \pmod{p} \quad \text{for all } 1 \leq k \leq \frac{p-1}{2}.
$$

Let $p$ be an odd prime number. Find all $\frac{p-1}{2}$-tuples $(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{\frac{p-1}{2}}) \in \mathbb{Z}_{p^2}^{\frac{p-1}{2}}$ such that
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{\frac{p-1}{2}} x_i^k \equiv 0 \pmod{p^2} \quad \text{for all } 1 \leq k \leq \frac{p-1}{2}.
$$

Let $p$ be an odd prime number. Find all $\frac{p-1}{2}$-tuples $(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{\frac{p-1}{2}}) \in \mathbb{Z}_{p^2}^{\frac{p-1}{2}}$ such that
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{\frac{p-1}{2}} x_i^k > 0 \quad \text{for all } 1 \leq k \leq \frac{p-1}{2}.
$$
